metadata.visit_title: Wound check after laparoscopic cholecystectomy

reasonCode.text: Postoperative incision concern

Observation.valueString: Umbilical incision minimally separated superficially with scant serous drainage; no erythema, warmth, purulence, fluctuance, or fascial defect.

CarePlan.title: Postoperative incision care

detail.description: Daily dry dressing, no immersion, lifting restriction, photo follow-up in 72 hours.

transcript:
Medical assistant: Nikhil, you are one week out from laparoscopic gallbladder removal. What brought you in before your scheduled two-week visit?

Patient: This morning the bandage at my belly button had a pale yellow spot. I sent a photo, and the nurse offered a wound check. I was worried the incision opened.

Medical assistant: Any fever, chills, worsening belly pain, vomiting, bad smell, or thick drainage?

Patient: None. My temperature was normal. Pain is two out of ten and improving. I am eating regular food, passing gas, and having bowel movements.

PA Lee: Hi, Nikhil. I reviewed the operative report. Your laparoscopic cholecystectomy on July eleventh was uncomplicated. Tell me about activity since then.

Patient: I walked every day. Yesterday I carried two grocery bags up one flight. They may have been heavier than the instructions allowed. Later I noticed a pulling feeling near the belly button, then the small wet spot this morning.

PA Lee: Thank you. I am removing the dressing now. The three upper incisions are closed, dry, and without redness. At the umbilical incision, the skin edges are separated by about three millimeters at the surface only. There is a tiny amount of clear straw-colored fluid. I do not see pus, spreading redness, warmth, a pocket of fluid, or a deeper fascial opening. Your abdomen is soft and only mildly tender near the incision. Temperature is 36.7 Celsius. This looks like superficial drainage, not infection or a hernia.

Patient: Do I need stitches or antibiotics?

PA Lee: No. Closing a draining surface with stitches could trap fluid, and the gap is small enough to heal from the base. Antibiotics do not help when there are no signs of bacterial infection. I will gently rinse with sterile saline, pat it dry, place a narrow adhesive strip across the edges without pulling tightly, and cover it with dry gauze.

Patient: Should I use hydrogen peroxide or antibiotic ointment at home?

PA Lee: Please do not use peroxide, alcohol, iodine, powders, or ointment unless the surgical team directs it; those can irritate healing tissue or keep it too moist. Starting tomorrow, shower normally, let mild soap and water run over the area, do not scrub, and pat dry with a clean towel. Replace dry gauze once daily and whenever damp. Leave the adhesive strip in place until it loosens on its own.

Patient: I have a desk job. Can I work Monday?

PA Lee: Yes, if you feel comfortable and can take walking breaks. Avoid lifting, pushing, or pulling more than ten pounds until two weeks after surgery, then increase gradually if the incision remains dry and pain does not increase. No abdominal workouts yet. Do not soak in a bath, pool, or hot tub until all incisions are fully sealed with no drainage for at least forty-eight hours. Walking and stairs are encouraged.

Patient: I stopped the oxycodone after the first night. I alternate acetaminophen and ibuprofen sometimes.

PA Lee: That is appropriate if used within the labeled doses and you have no contraindications. Take ibuprofen with food. Pain should keep trending down. Avoid driving if pain limits sudden movement or while taking any sedating medicine.

Patient: What changes mean I should call tonight?

PA Lee: Call the surgical line the same day for spreading redness, increasing warmth or swelling, thick yellow or green drainage, bad odor, pain that is clearly worsening, persistent vomiting, or temperature at or above 100.4 Fahrenheit. Go to the emergency department for severe or rapidly increasing abdominal pain, a firm new bulge at the incision, uncontrolled bleeding, fainting, chest pain, or trouble breathing. A little clear or pink moisture today can be normal; gauze that becomes repeatedly saturated is not.

Medical assistant: We will send a secure message in three days. Please reply with a well-lit photo, or sooner if anything changes. Keep the routine postoperative appointment next Friday so the surgeon can review healing and final pathology.

Patient: Let me repeat it. Shower, pat dry, dry gauze, no peroxide or ointment, and no lifting over ten pounds. I call for redness, pus, fever, worse pain, or saturated dressings. I can walk and do desk work.

PA Lee: Exactly. The wound is shallow and clean today. Your questions were appropriate, and I expect uncomplicated healing with protection from strain.
note:
POSTOPERATIVE WOUND-CHECK NOTE

Nikhil Patel is a 40-year-old man postoperative day 7 after uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis. He requested an early wound check after noticing scant pale-yellow drainage on the umbilical dressing this morning. He carried grocery bags yesterday and felt brief pulling at the site. He denies fever, chills, worsening abdominal pain, vomiting, malodor, purulent drainage, or change in bowel function. He is tolerating a regular diet, walking daily, and no longer uses oxycodone. Pain is 2/10 and improving.

Exam: Temperature 36.7 C. Well appearing. Abdomen soft, nondistended, with expected mild peri-incisional tenderness and no rebound or guarding. Three superior port incisions are closed, clean, and dry. Umbilical skin edges have approximately 3 mm superficial separation with scant serous drainage. No erythema, warmth, induration, fluctuance, purulence, malodor, active bleeding, palpable hernia, or fascial defect.

Assessment: Minor superficial umbilical port-site separation with serous drainage after increased lifting. No evidence of surgical-site infection, abscess, dehiscence below skin, or incisional hernia. Antibiotics, imaging, and re-closure are not indicated.

Plan: Site rinsed with sterile saline and dried. A loose adhesive strip and dry gauze were applied. Beginning tomorrow, shower with mild soap and water, avoid scrubbing, and pat dry. Replace dry gauze daily and whenever damp; allow adhesive strip to detach naturally. Avoid peroxide, alcohol, iodine, powders, and topical ointments. No lifting, pushing, or pulling over 10 pounds until postoperative day 14, then advance gradually if dry and comfortable. Walking, stairs, and desk work are permitted. No bathing, swimming, or hot tub until every incision is sealed and drainage-free for at least 48 hours. Continue acetaminophen or ibuprofen within labeled limits as needed.

Send a well-lit wound photo through the secure portal in 72 hours and keep scheduled surgical follow-up next Friday. Call same day for spreading redness, warmth, swelling, purulent or foul drainage, worsening pain, repeated saturation of gauze, persistent vomiting, or temperature at or above 100.4 F. Seek emergency care for severe rapidly worsening abdominal pain, firm new bulge, uncontrolled bleeding, syncope, chest pain, or dyspnea. Patient completed teach-back.
after_visit_summary: Your belly-button incision has a small, shallow opening with clear drainage but no signs of infection or deeper separation. Shower with mild soap and water, pat dry, and replace dry gauze daily or when damp. Leave the adhesive strip until it loosens. Do not use peroxide, alcohol, iodine, powder, or ointment. Lift no more than 10 pounds until two weeks after surgery; walking and desk work are okay. Send a wound photo in 72 hours and keep next Friday's visit. Call for spreading redness, pus, bad odor, fever of 100.4 F or higher, worsening pain, vomiting, or saturated gauze. Seek emergency care for severe pain, a firm bulge, heavy bleeding, fainting, chest pain, or breathing trouble.

metadata.visit_title: Bicycle fall with mild concussion

reasonCode.text: Head injury after bicycle fall

code.text: Mild concussion without loss of consciousness

DiagnosticReport.conclusion: No acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass effect, or skull fracture.

dosageInstruction.text: Take 1 to 2 tablets by mouth every 6 hours as needed for headache; maximum 3000 mg daily.

transcript:
Nurse: Eli, I am checking you again before the doctor comes back. Tell me what happened in your own words.

Patient: I was riding home in the bike lane. A car door opened, I swerved, and went over the handlebars. I hit the right side of my helmet and slid on my elbow. I did not black out.

Nurse: Any vomiting, double vision, neck pain, weakness, or numbness?

Patient: No vomiting or vision trouble. I felt stunned for maybe a minute and I have a dull headache. I was a little queasy in the ambulance, but that is gone. My neck feels normal.

Nurse: Your helmet cracked, so I am glad you wore it. Your blood pressure is 128 over 76, pulse 82, and your neurologic checks have stayed normal. Your roommate is in the waiting room and can take you home.

Patient: Yes, Jordan can stay with me tonight. I have an exam tomorrow.

Dr. Shah: Hi, Eli. I reviewed the paramedic report and examined you earlier. I want to repeat a few questions. What month is it, where are we, and what happened?

Patient: July 2026, Bay City Emergency, and I crashed after avoiding a car door.

Dr. Shah: Correct. Follow my finger. Smile, lift both arms, and push your feet against my hands. Everything is symmetric. Your Glasgow Coma Scale is fifteen. The elbow scrape is superficial, and the joint moves fully without focal bone tenderness. We cleaned it and your tetanus vaccination is current.

Patient: Does the cracked helmet mean I have bleeding in my brain?

Dr. Shah: The helmet absorbed force; it does not by itself prove bleeding. Because of the impact and persistent headache, we obtained a CT scan. It shows no bleeding, swelling, skull fracture, or other acute abnormality. Your history and symptoms fit a mild concussion. Symptoms such as headache, fatigue, mild nausea, slowed concentration, irritability, or light sensitivity can appear over the next day or two. Most improve gradually.

Patient: Can I sleep tonight? My mom says people with concussions cannot sleep.

Dr. Shah: You may sleep. Jordan should stay nearby and check that you can be awakened normally if concerned. You do not need hourly alarms if you are resting comfortably. Return immediately or call emergency services for a worsening severe headache, repeated vomiting, unusual confusion, seizure, fainting, trouble waking, slurred speech, new weakness or numbness, unequal pupils, or fluid or blood from the nose or ears.

Patient: What about the exam and riding again?

Dr. Shah: Skip the exam tomorrow and ask for an academic accommodation. For the first twenty-four to forty-eight hours, use relative rest: normal light activity at home is fine, but stop if symptoms clearly worsen. Limit prolonged screens, loud environments, alcohol, cannabis, and driving. Do not bike, run hard, lift heavily, or play contact sports. After a day or two, add light walking and increase activity stepwise as tolerated. No activity with risk of another head impact until symptom-free and cleared. Replace the helmet.

Patient: Can I take ibuprofen?

Dr. Shah: Tonight, use acetaminophen, five hundred to one thousand milligrams every six hours if needed, with no more than three thousand milligrams in twenty-four hours. Avoid combining it with cold medicines containing acetaminophen. Since your scan is reassuring, ibuprofen is generally reasonable after the first twenty-four hours if you have no stomach, kidney, or bleeding problems, but acetaminophen is the simplest first choice.

Nurse: I have written instructions for you and Jordan. We scheduled a concussion clinic or primary-care check within three to five days. Keep the elbow clean with soap and water, apply a thin layer of petroleum ointment, and cover it until dry. Watch for spreading redness, pus, fever, or increasing pain.

Patient: I understand. Headache getting much worse, vomiting, confusion, weakness, seizure, or being hard to wake means come back. Jordan stays tonight, no exam, no bike, and gradual activity.

Dr. Shah: Exactly. Your repeat examination is stable, you are walking normally, and you are safe for discharge with supervision.
note:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT NOTE

Chief concern: Head injury after bicycle fall.

HPI: Eli Brooks is a 21-year-old man brought by EMS after swerving to avoid an opened car door and falling over bicycle handlebars. He struck the right helmeted head; helmet cracked. He denies loss of consciousness, amnesia, vomiting, seizure, neck pain, vision change, focal weakness, or numbness. He reports transient nausea that resolved and a persistent dull headache. Roommate is available for discharge supervision.

Exam: BP 128/76, pulse 82. Alert and oriented, GCS 15. Speech clear. Pupils equal and reactive; extraocular movements intact. Face symmetric. Strength and sensation intact in all extremities. Normal gait. No midline cervical tenderness. Superficial right elbow abrasion without deformity or focal bony tenderness; full range of motion. Serial neurologic examinations remained stable.

Diagnostics: CT head without contrast shows no acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass effect, or skull fracture.

Assessment: 1. Mild concussion without loss of consciousness. 2. Superficial right elbow abrasion. Presentation is reassuring against intracranial injury given normal CT, stable GCS, and nonfocal serial examinations. No indication for admission.

Plan: Discharge home with roommate supervising tonight. Relative cognitive and physical rest for 24-48 hours, followed by gradual return to light activity as tolerated. Avoid driving, alcohol, cannabis, strenuous exercise, cycling, contact sports, and any risk of repeat head injury until symptom-free and medically cleared. Provide school excuse and arrange primary-care or concussion-clinic follow-up in 3-5 days. Acetaminophen 500-1000 mg every 6 hours as needed, maximum 3000 mg/day; avoid duplicate acetaminophen products. Clean elbow daily with soap and water, apply petroleum ointment, and cover until dry. Replace damaged helmet.

Return precautions reviewed verbally and in writing: worsening severe headache, repeated vomiting, increasing confusion, seizure, syncope, difficulty awakening, slurred speech, unequal pupils, new weakness or numbness, or blood/fluid from nose or ears. Patient accurately used teach-back and agrees with plan.

Rest relatively for 24-48 hours, then increase light activity gradually. Do not drive, bike, play contact sports, drink alcohol, or risk another head impact until symptom-free and cleared. Use acetaminophen as directed and keep the elbow clean and covered. Have your roommate stay with you tonight and follow up in 3-5 days. Return now for worsening severe headache, repeated vomiting, confusion, seizure, fainting, trouble waking, slurred speech, unequal pupils, or new weakness/numbness.

metadata.visit_title: Discharge after community-acquired pneumonia

reasonCode.text: Fever, cough, and hypoxemia

DiagnosticReport.conclusion: Patchy right lower lobe airspace opacity compatible with pneumonia.

dosageInstruction.text: Take one tablet by mouth twice daily with food for 3 days.
Take one tablet by mouth daily for 2 days.

CarePlan.title: Pneumonia discharge recovery plan

detail.description: Complete oral antibiotics, use incentive spirometer, walk regularly, and follow up within one week.

transcript:
RN Kim: Ms. Ramirez, your daughter Elena is here. With your permission, I would like us to review the discharge plan together and use the Spanish interpreter on the tablet.

Patient: Yes, please. Elena helps me organize the pills, but I want to understand them too.

Interpreter: I will interpret everything said. Please speak directly to Ms. Ramirez.

RN Kim: You came in three nights ago with fever, cough, shortness of breath, and a low oxygen level. Today your temperature is normal, breathing rate is eighteen, and oxygen saturation is ninety-five percent while walking on room air. You have not needed oxygen since yesterday morning. How do you feel compared with admission?

Patient: Much better. I still cough and feel tired when I walk, but I am not gasping. I ate breakfast.

Elena: She looks more like herself. Is the infection gone, or could it come back tonight?

Dr. Bennett: The chest x-ray showed pneumonia in the right lower lung. Blood cultures have no growth at forty-eight hours. She improved with ceftriaxone and azithromycin in the hospital, has been without fever, and passed the walking oxygen check. Those findings make discharge appropriate. The cough and low energy can last days to a few weeks even while the infection is clearing. We are switching from intravenous therapy to pills to complete the course.

Patient: Which pills are new? I already take losartan and metformin.

RN Kim: The first is amoxicillin-clavulanate, eight hundred seventy-five slash one hundred twenty-five milligrams: one tablet with breakfast and one with dinner for three more days. The second is azithromycin, two hundred fifty milligrams: one tablet daily for two more days. Finish both even if you feel well. Taking the first with food may reduce stomach upset. Call if diarrhea is severe or watery, you develop a rash, or you cannot keep medicine down.

Elena: So tonight she takes the amoxicillin-clavulanate with dinner, but no azithromycin until tomorrow morning?

RN Kim: Correct; today's azithromycin was already given. I marked each dose on the calendar. Please continue losartan fifty milligrams daily. Resume metformin five hundred milligrams twice daily with meals because kidney function and eating have returned to baseline. Check glucose before breakfast and dinner for the next several days; illness can temporarily raise it.

Patient: I have no oxygen tank at home. Are you sure I do not need one?

Dr. Bennett: You do not meet a need for home oxygen now. Your saturation stayed at or above ninety-three percent during the hallway walk. Rest when tired, but get up for short walks several times daily. Use the incentive spirometer ten slow breaths every hour while awake for the next week. Drink fluids unless another clinician has restricted them.

Elena: What should make us return instead of waiting for the clinic?

Dr. Bennett: Call emergency services for severe trouble breathing, blue lips, fainting, new confusion, or chest pressure that does not pass. Return promptly for breathing that is clearly worsening, oxygen below ninety percent if you happen to measure it, repeated vomiting, inability to take antibiotics, coughing blood, or a fever of one hundred one degrees Fahrenheit or higher that returns and persists. Do not delay because of the weekend.

metadata.visit_title: Six-week postpartum follow-up — depression, anxiety, recovery, and lactation

reasonCode.text: Six-week postpartum assessment

coding.display: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale total score

dosageInstruction.text: Take 25 mg by mouth daily for 7 days, then 50 mg daily

CarePlan.title: Postpartum mood, lactation, and recovery plan

detail.description: Sertraline initiation, therapy referral, safety plan, and lactation follow-up

transcript:
NURSE: Mai, congratulations. Before Dr. Alvarez comes in, I have blood pressure 112 over 70, pulse 74, weight 68.1 kilograms, and pain one out of ten. You completed both mood forms. Is the baby with you today?
PT: My husband is walking her in the courtyard. She only likes the stroller if it keeps moving.
NURSE: Your Edinburgh score is 14 and your GAD-7 is 11. You marked never on the self-harm question. Is that still accurate right now?
PT: Yes. I do not want to hurt myself or the baby. I just do not feel like myself.
NURSE: Thank you. Dr. Alvarez will talk through that carefully.
DR: Hi, Mai. It is good to see you six weeks out. How is Linh doing?
PT: She is gaining weight now. The first two weeks were scary because she lost almost ten percent, but the pediatrician says she is back on her curve.
DR: And how is your body recovering from the vaginal delivery and second-degree tear?
PT: Bleeding stopped about ten days ago. No fever or bad-smelling discharge. The stitches do not hurt, just a little pulling if I sit a long time. Urinating is normal. I am constipated sometimes, and I leak a few drops if I sneeze.
DR: Any heavy bleeding—soaking a pad in an hour—large clots, worsening pelvic pain, leg swelling, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe headache, or vision change?
PT: No.
DR: Breastfeeding?
PT: Mostly. She nurses eight or nine times a day, and my husband gives one bottle of pumped milk at night. My left nipple cracked early but healed. No red hot breast or fever. Supply feels lower in the evening, and that makes me panic.
DR: Evening cluster feeding is common and does not necessarily mean low supply. Are wet diapers and weight gain reassuring?
PT: Six or more wet diapers, and yes, she gained at the last two checks.
DR: We can arrange lactation follow-up for reassurance and positioning. Now I want to focus on you. What does not feeling like yourself look like?
PT: I cry almost every day, sometimes because the dishwasher is full. I love the baby, but I do not feel joy the way I expected. I lie down when she sleeps and then listen for every sound instead of sleeping.
DR: How long has that been happening?
PT: The first week was emotional but manageable. Around week three it got heavier.
DR: Worry themes?
PT: That she will stop breathing, that I will drop her on the stairs, that my milk will disappear. I check her breathing over and over. I know the thoughts are too much, but knowing does not stop them.
DR: Are these unwanted scary thoughts, or do you believe you should act on them?
PT: Unwanted. I do not want anything bad to happen. I have never thought about hurting her.
DR: Any time you hear voices others do not, feel watched, become unusually energized with little need for sleep, have racing grand plans, feel confused, or believe the baby is possessed or sending special messages?
PT: No. Nothing like that. I am exhausted and worried, not energized.
DR: Any thoughts that you would be better off dead, wishing you would not wake up, or hurting yourself?
PT: No.
DR: Do you feel able to care for Linh safely?
PT: Yes. When I get overwhelmed, I put her safely in the crib and call my husband or my sister.
DR: That is an excellent safety strategy. Who is available regularly?
PT: My husband took four weeks off and is back at work. My mother comes Tuesdays and Thursdays. My sister lives fifteen minutes away. At night my husband does the pumped bottle.
DR: Any relationship safety concerns or anyone controlling or hurting you?
PT: No. My husband is supportive. He is tired too, but kind.
DR: You had anxiety in graduate school. What treatment helped then?
PT: Therapy helped. I took sertraline, I think 50 milligrams, for about a year. It worked. I stopped before trying to get pregnant and did fine until now.
DR: Any side effects then? Any history of bipolar disorder, mania, or psychiatric hospitalization?
PT: Mild nausea the first week. No bipolar or hospital stays.
DR: Your EPDS score of 14 and GAD-7 of 11, plus persistent low mood, reduced enjoyment, sleep disruption beyond the baby’s schedule, and intrusive worry, support postpartum depression and anxiety—not a personal failure and not simply something you must wait out.
PT: I feel guilty because we wanted her so much.
DR: Wanting and loving your baby do not immunize anyone against postpartum depression. This is common and treatable. Therapy and medication are both appropriate at this level, especially since sertraline helped before.
PT: I am worried medicine will get into breast milk or lower supply.
DR: Sertraline passes into milk in very small amounts and is commonly preferred during breastfeeding. No medication is zero-exposure, but untreated depression and anxiety also affect sleep, bonding, and function. Available evidence and your prior response make sertraline a reasonable choice. It is not generally expected to lower milk supply directly. We will monitor you and the baby.
PT: What should I watch for in her?
DR: Unusual sleepiness, feeding difficulty, irritability, or poor weight gain would be reasons to call the pediatrician, though significant effects are uncommon. Continue routine weight checks.
PT: And for me?
DR: Start 25 milligrams each morning for seven days, then 50 milligrams daily. Taking it with food may reduce nausea. Early effects can include stomach upset, headache, jitteriness, or sleep change; benefits build over two to six weeks. Do not stop abruptly without contacting us. Rarely, antidepressants can increase agitation or suicidal thoughts early, so call promptly for a marked worsening.
PT: Can I take it at night?
DR: You may switch timing if it makes you sleepy, but start in the morning because it was neutral for you before. I am also placing an urgent—not emergency—referral to our perinatal therapist. They should call within three business days.
PT: That would help. I keep trying to explain this to friends, and they say every new mom is tired.
DR: Fatigue is universal; daily crying and persistent loss of pleasure deserve care. I want a concrete rest plan. Could your mother cover one uninterrupted three-hour block on Tuesdays and Thursdays while you sleep away from the monitor?
PT: Yes, if I can make myself turn it off.
DR: Your mother can bring the baby to you for feeding if needed, or you can leave expressed milk. One protected block is treatment, not indulgence. Continue the overnight bottle arrangement.
DR: Let us review emergency signs. If you develop thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, feel unable to keep either of you safe, hear voices, become severely confused, or go days with almost no sleep and unusually high energy, do not wait for a clinic message. Call 988 or 911, go to the emergency department, and have a trusted adult stay with you and the baby.
PT: I can tell my husband and sister the warning signs.
DR: Please do. For non-emergency worsening, call our same-day line. We will have a nurse call in three days and see you in two weeks, sooner if needed.
PT: That feels much sooner than the usual yearly visit, which is good.
DR: Absolutely. Now contraception—have you resumed sex or made a plan?
PT: Not yet. We want to wait at least two years before another pregnancy. I was thinking about the progestin-only pill because I am breastfeeding.
DR: That is compatible with lactation, but it must be taken at nearly the same time daily. Long-acting options such as an IUD or implant are also compatible. Do you want a prescription today?
PT: I want to discuss the IUD with my husband and decide at the two-week visit. Condoms until then.
DR: Reasonable. Fertility can return before the first period, so use condoms every time.
DR: On exam, the perineal repair is well healed without infection or separation. Mild pelvic floor weakness fits the stress leakage. I recommend pelvic floor exercises—ten slow contractions, three sets daily—and pelvic floor physical therapy if it is not improving. Resume activity gradually based on comfort. Lubricant can help with postpartum dryness when you resume sex.
PT: Is exercise okay? I miss walking alone.
DR: Yes. Start with ten to fifteen minutes and build gradually; walking can support mood. Stop and call for increased bleeding or significant pain. Continue prenatal vitamin while breastfeeding, hydrate to thirst, and eat regular meals.
PT: What about the supply worry at night?
DR: Watch the baby, not the pump volume: swallowing, wet diapers, and growth are the best indicators. The lactation consultant can observe a feed. Avoid unregulated herbal mood or milk-supply products because ingredients and interactions vary.
NURSE: I can schedule the two-week video follow-up and give her the crisis card.
DR: Thank you. Mai, can you summarize the plan?
PT: Start sertraline 25 for a week, then 50. Therapy should call. My mom will cover protected sleep twice a week. Lactation will check a feeding. My husband and sister get the emergency signs. Nurse call in three days, visit in two weeks. Condoms until we decide contraception.
DR: Exactly. You are not alone, and we are not asking you to manage this alone.
note:
**Subjective:** Mai Nguyen is a 30-year-old G1P1 at six weeks postpartum after uncomplicated vaginal delivery with repaired second-degree perineal laceration. Lochia ended ten days ago; no fever, foul discharge, heavy bleeding, pelvic pain, cardiopulmonary symptoms, or hypertensive warning symptoms. Mild stress urinary leakage and intermittent constipation are present. She is predominantly breastfeeding with one nightly bottle of expressed milk; infant has at least six wet diapers daily and appropriate recent weight gain. Prior nipple fissure healed; no mastitis symptoms.

Since approximately postpartum week three she has had daily crying, reduced pleasure, guilt, insomnia beyond infant waking, hypervigilant checking, and intrusive unwanted fears about accidental infant harm. She firmly denies desire or intent to harm infant, suicidal ideation, passive death wish, hallucinations, delusions, confusion, mania, or inability to provide safe care. She uses the crib and calls family when overwhelmed. Husband, mother, and sister are supportive; no intimate-partner violence. Prior anxiety responded well to therapy and sertraline 50 mg without mania.

**Objective:** BP 112/70 mmHg, HR 74/min, weight 68.1 kg, pain 1/10. EPDS 14, self-harm item 0; GAD-7 11. Tearful but engaged, linear, future-oriented, normal speech, no psychosis. Perineal repair well healed without separation or infection. Mild pelvic floor weakness. Breast examination without erythema or focal tenderness.

**Assessment:**
1. Postpartum depression and anxiety, moderate, without suicidality, psychosis, mania, or current safety impairment. Protective supports and insight are strong.
2. Lactating mother with reassuring infant output/growth and evening supply worry; no mastitis.
3. Routine postpartum recovery with healed laceration and mild stress incontinence.
4. Contraceptive counseling.

**Plan:**
- Start sertraline 25 mg daily with food for 7 days, then 50 mg daily. Prior benefit and low infant exposure in lactation reviewed. Discussed early GI, sleep, or activation effects and 2-6 week benefit onset. Do not stop abruptly. Monitor infant for unusual sedation, feeding difficulty, irritability, or poor weight gain and contact pediatrician if present.
- Urgent perinatal therapy referral; expected contact within 3 business days. Protected three-hour sleep block with mother twice weekly and continued partner overnight bottle. Nurse safety check in 3 days; mood follow-up in 2 weeks.
- Safety plan shared with husband and sister. For thoughts of harming self/baby, inability to maintain safety, hallucinations, severe confusion, or marked sleepless high energy: trusted adult stays with patient/baby and patient calls 988/911 or goes to ED. Same-day clinic line for non-emergency worsening.
- Lactation consultation for observed feed. Follow infant output and growth rather than pump volume; avoid unregulated supplements. Continue prenatal vitamin and hydrate to thirst.
- Pelvic floor contractions, 10 slow repetitions three sets daily; consider pelvic floor PT if persistent. Gradual walking/activity; stop and call for increased bleeding or significant pain.
- Condoms with every intercourse until contraception decision; discuss IUD versus progestin-only pill at two-week visit.
after_visit_summary:
Visit summary

What we discussed
• Postpartum depression and anxiety
• Breastfeeding and milk-supply concerns
• Recovery from delivery and pelvic floor weakness
• Contraception

Next steps
• Start sertraline 25 mg daily with food for 7 days, then 50 mg daily. Do not stop abruptly.
• Watch the baby for unusual sleepiness, feeding difficulty, irritability, or poor weight gain and call the pediatrician if these occur.
• Perinatal therapy should contact you within 3 business days. Nurse safety call in 3 days; mood follow-up in 2 weeks.
• Arrange protected three-hour sleep blocks twice weekly. Lactation consultation was placed.
• Call 988/911 or go to the emergency department for thoughts of harming yourself or the baby, inability to keep either of you safe, hallucinations, severe confusion, or unusually high energy with almost no sleep.
• Perform 10 slow pelvic-floor contractions three times daily and resume walking gradually.
• Use condoms every time until choosing longer-term contraception at follow-up.

transcript:
Medical assistant: Hello, Arthur. Before Dr. Isabel Moreno comes in, please tell me what has changed since your last visit.

Patient: Overall things are stable. I have had morning stiffness improves within forty minutes of the first dose but returns before dinner. I brought my medication list.

Medical assistant: Have you missed medicine or noticed side effects? Any urgent symptoms?

Patient: I have taken Carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 mg three times daily as directed. I report no falls, hallucinations, fainting, swallowing difficulty, or uncontrolled movements. I wanted to make sure the remaining symptoms do not mean the condition is getting worse.

Dr. Isabel Moreno: I reviewed your history, medicines, and recent results. What matters most to you right now?

Patient: I can handle usual activities, but sometimes worry about what is safe. I want to stay independent and know when to call.

Dr. Isabel Moreno: Today's examination shows mild right resting tremor and bradykinesia; rises without arms; gait narrow with reduced right arm swing. Testing is reassuring overall: timed up-and-go was 10.8 seconds while on medication. Together, this supports Parkinson disease without dyskinesia being stable for outpatient management. Nothing today requires emergency treatment.

Patient: Should I change the medicine now? I prefer not to add treatment unless the benefit is clear.

Dr. Isabel Moreno: The plan is to move the third levodopa dose one hour earlier, continue exercise, and begin speech-volume practice. Do not stop or double prescription medicine without contacting us. If a dose is missed, follow the label or call.

Patient: Is normal activity okay?

Dr. Isabel Moreno: Continue comfortable activity and increase gradually. Pace yourself, use prescribed assistive devices, and stop if symptoms differ distinctly from your usual pattern. Consistent sleep, balanced meals, and avoiding tobacco support treatment. Ask before starting supplements.

Patient: What should I track between visits?

Dr. Isabel Moreno: Record symptoms, medication timing, triggers, and effects on function. Bring the log to movement-disorders clinic in three months. Complete ordered tests on schedule. Contact us earlier if symptoms become more frequent, intense, or limiting.

Patient: Which symptoms should send me for urgent help?

Dr. Isabel Moreno: Seek urgent or emergency care for new inability to walk, repeated falls with injury, choking, severe confusion, hallucinations causing danger, or fainting. For a concerning but nonemergency change, call our clinic the same day. Do not wait for the planned follow-up if you feel unsafe.

Medical assistant: I will print the plan and confirm the testing instructions. The portal message will include the clinic number and follow-up timing.

Patient: Let me repeat it back. I will continue the agreed treatment, complete the monitoring, keep a symptom and medication log, and return for movement-disorders clinic in three months. I will call sooner for a meaningful change and seek urgent help for the warning signs we discussed.

Dr. Isabel Moreno: Correct. Your teach-back is accurate, and your questions are welcome.
note:
SPECIALTY FOLLOW-UP NOTE

Arthur Green is a 74-year-old male patient seen for follow-up of Parkinson disease without dyskinesia. Since the last visit, he reports morning stiffness improves within forty minutes of the first dose but returns before dinner. Medication reconciliation confirms Carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 mg three times daily as directed. He reports no falls, hallucinations, fainting, swallowing difficulty, or uncontrolled movements. Function remains adequate for routine home and community activities, and the patient requests specific monitoring and safety guidance.

Focused examination: Mild right resting tremor and bradykinesia; rises without arms; gait narrow with reduced right arm swing. Relevant data reviewed today: timed up-and-go was 10.8 seconds while on medication. Medication list, allergies, prior specialty documentation, and patient-maintained symptom notes were reviewed.

Assessment: Parkinson disease without dyskinesia. Current history, examination, and available testing support continued outpatient management. No acute instability was identified today. Remaining symptoms and longer-term risks were discussed using shared decision-making, including the benefits and burdens of changing therapy now.

Plan: move the third levodopa dose one hour earlier, continue exercise, and begin speech-volume practice. Continue other established medicines unless changed by their prescriber. Do not stop, double, or share prescription treatment. Maintain a dated log of symptoms, medication timing, triggers, and functional effect. Continue comfortable activity with gradual progression and condition-specific precautions. Avoid tobacco and check with the care team before adding supplements. Complete ordered monitoring on schedule and return to movement-disorders clinic in three months; contact the clinic earlier for increasing frequency, severity, medication intolerance, or loss of function.

Urgent precautions reviewed: seek urgent or emergency care for new inability to walk, repeated falls with injury, choking, severe confusion, hallucinations causing danger, or fainting. Patient voiced understanding, completed teach-back, and agrees with the plan.
after_visit_summary: Today we reviewed Parkinson disease without dyskinesia. Move the third levodopa dose one hour earlier, continue exercise, and begin speech-volume practice. transcript:
FAMILY: We wrote down the pattern at home so we could give an accurate history.

PT: My main question is how to manage polycystic ovary syndrome without making unnecessary changes.

PT OLIVIA STONE: I reviewed the history carefully. Important negatives are: No severe pelvic pain, heavy current bleeding, vision change, galactorrhea, or pregnancy symptoms. That lowers concern for an emergency today, although it does not replace the safety plan.

PT: What did today's examination or testing show?

PT OLIVIA STONE: Irregular cycles with clinical hirsutism; pregnancy test negative. Taken with the history, this supports polycystic ovary syndrome. I do not see a current indication for emergency transfer or broad testing beyond the focused plan we discussed.

PT: Please explain the treatment and what I should expect.

PT OLIVIA STONE: The treatment decision is: Combined oral contraceptive after shared contraindication review. We reviewed the expected benefit, common burdens, practical alternatives, and how personal preferences affect the choice. Do not add extra doses or share treatment with anyone.

PT: What should I do at home in addition to that?

PT OLIVIA STONE: Track bleeding, pursue sustainable activity and nutrition goals, and discuss fertility timing openly. Make one sustainable change at a time and record symptoms, adherence, or barriers. That record will help us decide whether the plan is effective rather than relying on a single good or bad day.

MA: Could you repeat the plan in your own words before leaving?

PT: I will use the treatment as directed, follow the home steps, keep the requested record, and contact the clinic before making an unplanned change.

PT OLIVIA STONE: Correct. The follow-up plan is to blood-pressure check in three months. At that point we will review response, side effects, access, and whether the diagnosis or plan needs adjustment.

PT: Which symptoms should not wait for that appointment?

PT OLIVIA STONE: Seek prompt assessment for chest pain, shortness of breath, one-sided leg swelling, severe headache, vision change, or very heavy bleeding. For immediately life-threatening symptoms, call emergency services. For nonurgent questions, unexpected effects, or difficulty obtaining treatment, contact the clinic during office hours.

PT: That is clear. I agree with the plan and know where to find the written instructions.

metadata.visit_title: Acute right otitis media with parent present

reasonCode.text: Ear pain and fever

dosageInstruction.text: Give 10 mL by mouth twice daily for 7 days

CarePlan.title: Otitis media home care

detail.description: Antibiotic, analgesia, hydration, and return precautions

transcript:
MA: Eli, I like your dinosaur shirt. May I check your temperature and weight?
CHILD: Rex is the strongest one.
FATHER: He has been guarding that ear since last night.
MA: Temperature is 38.1 Celsius, weight 17.8 kilograms, oxygen 99 percent. Dr. Shah will be right in.
DR: Hi, Eli. Hi, Mr. Brooks. Tell me what started first.
FATHER: He had a runny nose four days ago. Yesterday after preschool he said his right ear hurt. Overnight he woke crying twice and felt warm. Our thermometer showed 101.4.
DR: Any drainage or blood from the ear?
FATHER: No. He says sounds are muffled, but he can hear me.
DR: Eli, does this ear hurt or itch?
CHILD: Hurt. Like somebody pushing.
DR: Any headache, stiff neck, dizziness, or trouble walking?
CHILD: No.
FATHER: No balance problem. He has been tired but alert.
DR: Vomiting, diarrhea, rash, cough, trouble breathing, or pain behind the ear?
FATHER: None. He ate half a banana and toast, and he is drinking. He urinated this morning.
DR: Has he had ear infections before?
FATHER: One at age two. Amoxicillin worked. No tubes and no hearing concerns.
DR: Any medication allergies or reaction to penicillin?
FATHER: No known allergies.
DR: What have you given for discomfort?
FATHER: Children's acetaminophen at two this morning, five milliliters. It helped for a few hours.
DR: We will calculate doses from today's weight. Eli, may I look in your ears? First I will look in Dad's ear light, then yours.
CHILD: Only if Dad holds Rex.
DR: Deal. The left canal and eardrum look normal. The right eardrum is red, bulging, and cloudy, and it does not move normally. There is no perforation. The canal is not swollen, and pressing the tragus does not hurt. Behind the ear there is no redness, swelling, or tenderness. His throat is mildly red without pus. Lungs are clear and neck is flexible.
FATHER: So it is an infection?
DR: Yes, acute middle-ear infection on the right after a viral cold. The bulging eardrum makes the diagnosis clear. He does not have findings of swimmer's ear or mastoid infection.
FATHER: Does he definitely need antibiotics? I have heard some can be watched.
DR: Observation can be reasonable in selected children with mild symptoms and reliable follow-up. Eli has significant overnight pain, fever, and a distinctly bulging membrane. Antibiotic treatment is reasonable. We can use high-dose amoxicillin because he has no allergy, no amoxicillin in the last month, and no purulent eye infection.
FATHER: What dose?
DR: Amoxicillin 400 milligrams per five milliliters: give ten milliliters by mouth twice daily for seven days. Shake well, measure with an oral syringe, and finish the course even if he feels better. Mild loose stool can occur. A widespread itchy rash, facial swelling, wheezing, or breathing difficulty needs prompt attention; breathing difficulty or facial swelling is an emergency.
FATHER: Can he take it with food?
DR: Yes, food may help stomach upset. For pain or fever, acetaminophen 160 milligrams per five milliliters: give 8.3 milliliters every six hours as needed. Or ibuprofen 100 milligrams per five milliliters: give 8.9 milliliters every six to eight hours as needed, with food. Do not alternate on a complicated schedule, do not exceed label limits, and avoid aspirin.
FATHER: He hates liquid medicine.
DR: Let him choose the syringe or small cup, aim the syringe toward the inside cheek, give small portions, and praise each step. Do not hide the entire dose in a full drink he may not finish.
CHILD: Can Rex have medicine?
DR: Rex gets pretend medicine only. You get the real medicine that helps your ear.
FATHER: When can he return to preschool?
DR: When fever-free for 24 hours without fever medicine and feeling well enough to participate. The ear infection itself is not spread person to person, but the cold virus is. Handwashing and covering coughs help.
FATHER: Should I keep water out of his ear?
DR: Normal bathing is fine because the eardrum is intact. No cotton swabs or drops unless we recommend them. Encourage fluids and rest. A warm compress can soothe the ear.
DR: Most pain and fever should improve within 48 to 72 hours. Call if he is not clearly improving by then, cannot keep medicine down, develops ear drainage, or symptoms worsen. Seek urgent care now for swelling or redness behind the ear, the ear sticking outward, severe headache, stiff neck, unusual sleepiness, trouble breathing, dehydration, or difficulty walking.
FATHER: Do we need a recheck?
DR: If he improves normally, no immediate recheck is required. If muffled hearing persists beyond several weeks, or infections become frequent, schedule follow-up.
DR: Mr. Brooks, can you repeat the plan?
FATHER: Ten milliliters of amoxicillin twice a day for seven days, measured carefully. Pain medicine based on your printed doses. Call if he is not better in two or three days, and get urgent help for swelling behind the ear, stiff neck, severe illness, or dehydration.
DR: Exactly. Eli, you did excellent work today.
CHILD: Rex did too.
note:
**Subjective:** Eli Brooks is a 4-year-old boy brought by his father for right ear pain beginning yesterday after four days of rhinorrhea. He woke crying twice overnight and had home temperature 101.4 F. He reports pressure-like pain and muffled sound without otorrhea. Father denies vomiting, diarrhea, rash, respiratory distress, headache, neck stiffness, disequilibrium, postauricular pain, or altered behavior. Oral intake is reduced but adequate; he drank and voided this morning. One remote otitis episode responded to amoxicillin. No tympanostomy history, hearing concern, recent antibiotics, medication allergy, or penicillin reaction. Acetaminophen provided temporary relief.

**Objective:** Temperature 38.1 C, weight 17.8 kg, SpO2 99%. Alert, interactive child. Right tympanic membrane erythematous, opaque, bulging, and hypomobile without perforation. Right canal is not edematous; no tragal tenderness. No mastoid erythema, swelling, displacement, or tenderness. Left ear normal. Mild pharyngeal erythema without exudate. Neck supple. Lungs clear with normal effort. Hydration clinically adequate.

**Assessment:** Acute right otitis media following viral upper respiratory infection. Significant pain, fever, and bulging membrane favor antibiotic treatment. No otitis externa, perforation, mastoiditis, respiratory compromise, or dehydration.

**Plan:** Start amoxicillin 400 mg/5 mL, 10 mL orally twice daily for 7 days. Shake, measure with an oral syringe, and complete the course. May give with food. Reviewed diarrhea and allergic-reaction precautions. For pain/fever, acetaminophen 160 mg/5 mL, 8.3 mL every 6 hours as needed, or ibuprofen 100 mg/5 mL, 8.9 mL every 6-8 hours as needed with food; avoid aspirin and complicated alternating schedules. Encourage fluids, rest, and warm compresses; no cotton swabs or unprescribed ear drops. Return to preschool after 24 hours fever-free without antipyretics and able to participate. Call if not clearly improving within 48-72 hours, medicine is not tolerated, drainage develops, or symptoms worsen. Seek urgent evaluation for postauricular swelling/redness, ear displacement, stiff neck, severe headache, unusual somnolence, breathing difficulty, dehydration, or gait change. Reassess persistent hearing change or recurrent infections.
after_visit_summary: Right middle-ear infection. Give amoxicillin 10 mL twice daily for 7 days and use the printed weight-based pain doses. Encourage fluids and rest. Call if not improving in 48-72 hours. Seek urgent help for swelling behind the ear, stiff neck, severe sleepiness, breathing trouble, dehydration, or trouble walking.

metadata.visit_title: Adolescent sports physical — exercise-induced asthma review

reasonCode.text: Preparticipation evaluation for school soccer

Observation.valueString: 20/20 both eyes without correction

dosageInstruction.text: Inhale 2 puffs with spacer 15 minutes before vigorous exercise; may use every 4 hours as needed for wheeze

transcript:
DR: Hi, Lucia. Hi, Ms. Morales. I understand this is the soccer physical.
PT: Yes. Tryouts start in three weeks, and the form has about a thousand boxes.
PARENT: She has been carrying it around like a winning lottery ticket.
DR: We will take good care of the boxes. Before we start, Lucia, I want you answering first whenever you can. Your mom can fill in details. What position do you play?
PT: Midfield, mostly. I run a lot, which is the point, but sometimes breathing gets annoying.
DR: Tell me exactly what annoying means.
PT: About ten minutes into hard drills my chest feels tight and I cough. Sometimes there is a little whistle when I breathe out. If I stop, it settles in maybe five minutes.
PARENT: Last season she came off the field twice. She looked scared, but her lips were never blue and she never passed out.
DR: Any symptoms sitting in class, overnight, or when you have a cold?
PT: Not sitting around. Maybe one night cough when I had a bad cold in January, but not normally.
DR: How often did you use albuterol last season?
PT: Only at games because I forgot it at practice. At games, two puffs before warm-up helped a lot.
PARENT: The prescription expired, and the inhaler has been through the washing machine once.
DR: That inhaler has retired. Did you use a spacer?
PT: No. I know I am supposed to.
DR: We will practice today. Any emergency visits, oral steroids, hospital stays, or intubation for asthma?
PARENT: None. She was diagnosed around age twelve after coughing during track.
DR: Any chest pain, racing heart, dizziness, fainting, or unusual exhaustion with exercise?
PT: No fainting. My heart pounds when everyone’s heart pounds. No pain.
DR: Has anyone in the family died suddenly during exercise or before age fifty from an unexplained heart problem? Any inherited rhythm condition or enlarged heart?
PARENT: No. Her grandfather had a heart attack at sixty-eight, but nothing young or unexplained.
DR: Good. Any seizures, concussion, neck injury, or heat illness?
PT: No. I rolled my right ankle two years ago, but physical therapy fixed it. It does not swell or give out.
DR: Any current joint pain?
PT: My legs get normal sore after conditioning, not injury sore.
DR: How are allergies?
PT: Spring was rough—sneezing and itchy eyes—but July is fine. I use cetirizine sometimes.
DR: Any medication allergies?
PARENT: None that we know of.
DR: Let us cover nutrition and recovery. What does a school day look like for food?
PT: Toast or cereal, school lunch, then something before practice. Usually a banana and peanut butter. Dinner at home.
PARENT: She skips breakfast when she is late.
PT: Twice, maybe. Not every day.
DR: Fluids?
PT: I carry a big bottle. Coach makes us weigh before and after hot practices, and we take breaks.
DR: Periods regular? Any very heavy bleeding, missed months, or trying to lose weight for sport?
PT: Regular, about every twenty-eight days. First day is crampy but manageable. I am not trying to lose weight.
DR: Sleep?
PT: Eight hours in summer. During school, closer to seven because homework exists.
DR: Mood and stress lately?
PT: Mostly good. I get nervous before tests and tryouts, but it passes. I still like my friends and soccer.
DR: I routinely spend a few minutes alone with teenagers. Ms. Morales, would you mind stepping out? We will bring you back before the exam is finished.
PARENT: Of course. I will tackle the school insurance page.
DR: Lucia, what you share is private unless I am worried someone is hurting you or you might hurt yourself. Do you feel safe at home, school, and with your team?
PT: Yes. My parents are strict about curfew, but safe. Coach is intense, not creepy.
DR: Any bullying?
PT: Some girls make comments online, but I block them. I have people I can talk to.
DR: Tobacco, vaping, alcohol, cannabis, pills, or supplements?
PT: No. A teammate vapes, and it smells awful. I use protein powder sometimes if my dad makes a smoothie, but no pre-workout stuff.
DR: Any sexual activity or questions about relationships?
PT: I am not sexually active. I am dating someone, but we have boundaries.
DR: Any persistent sadness, panic, thoughts of self-harm, or feeling that you would be better off dead?
PT: No.
DR: Great. Your vitals and growth look healthy: 164.2 centimeters, 55.8 kilograms, BMI 20.7, blood pressure 108 over 66, pulse 72, oxygen 99 percent. Vision is 20/20. I am going to listen to your heart and lungs, check strength and joints, then have your mom return.
PT: Okay.
DR: Deep breaths. Lungs are clear. Now squat, stand, hop on each foot. Any pain?
PT: No.
DR: Your ankle is stable, strength is symmetric, and there is no murmur lying down or standing. Ms. Morales can come back in.
PARENT: Did she pass the mysterious hopping test?
DR: With excellent form. I can clear her for soccer, with an asthma plan. Her history fits exercise-induced bronchoconstriction that responds to albuterol. There are no red flags for uncontrolled persistent asthma today.
PARENT: Does she need a daily inhaler?
DR: Not based on symptoms now. We will prescribe a fresh albuterol inhaler and spacer. Two puffs fifteen minutes before vigorous activity, including practice, not only games. She should keep it accessible rather than locked in the coach’s office.
PT: Can it stay in my soccer bag?
DR: Yes, protected from extreme heat, and tell coaches where it is. We will provide a school action plan. Let us review technique: shake it, attach spacer, breathe out, seal lips, press once, breathe in slowly and deeply, hold ten seconds, then wait about a minute before the second puff.
PT: I was doing both puffs back-to-back.
DR: The spacer and pause improve delivery. If you need albuterol more than twice a week outside planned pre-exercise use, wake at night coughing, or cannot keep up despite pretreatment, contact us. That may mean we need controller therapy or spirometry.
PARENT: What counts as an emergency?
DR: Severe trouble speaking, ribs pulling in, blue or gray lips, faintness, or symptoms not improving after rescue medication—call 911. Stop play for chest tightness or wheeze. Do not push through it.
PT: Coach sometimes says coughing is just being out of shape.
DR: Fitness and airway narrowing are different. Your plan should make that clear. Warm up gradually, especially in cold dry air, and use the rescue inhaler as directed.
PARENT: Do you recommend carrying two inhalers?
DR: One at school or in the sports bag and one at home is practical. Today’s prescription allows that. Check the dose counter monthly.
DR: Immunizations are current. I also recommend the annual influenza vaccine when available this fall and updated COVID vaccination according to the seasonal schedule. Wear shin guards, properly fitted cleats, and sunscreen; keep up hydration and regular meals.
PT: So the form says cleared?
DR: Cleared without restriction, provided albuterol is available and the asthma action plan is followed. I would like follow-up in three months, sooner if symptoms increase.
PARENT: We can do that.
PT: Thank you. I will try not to wash this inhaler.
note:
**Subjective:** Lucia Morales is a 15-year-old girl presenting with her mother for a school soccer preparticipation examination. She plays midfield. With hard drills she develops chest tightness, cough, and occasional expiratory wheeze about ten minutes into activity; symptoms resolve within approximately five minutes of rest and are substantially prevented by two puffs of albuterol before games. She has not consistently pretreated practices and did not use a spacer. No baseline daytime symptoms, routine nocturnal cough, emergency visits, systemic steroids, hospitalization, cyanosis, or syncope. Seasonal allergic rhinitis is mild currently. She denies exertional chest pain, unexplained fatigue, palpitations, dizziness, seizure, concussion, heat illness, or current musculoskeletal pain. Remote right ankle sprain resolved with physical therapy. Family history is negative for sudden unexplained death under age 50, inherited arrhythmia, or cardiomyopathy. Menses are regular without heavy bleeding; she denies restrictive eating. Private adolescent interview: safe at home, school, and on team; no tobacco, vaping, alcohol, cannabis, other substances, sexual activity, depression, self-harm thoughts, or suicidality.

**Objective:** Height 164.2 cm, weight 55.8 kg, BMI 20.7 kg/m2, BP 108/66 mmHg, HR 72/min, SpO2 99%. Vision 20/20 OU without correction. Well appearing and developmentally appropriate. Heart regular without murmur supine or standing. Lungs clear with normal work of breathing. Abdomen soft and nontender. Full painless cervical, shoulder, hip, knee, and ankle range of motion; symmetric strength; stable right ankle; normal single-leg hop and squat. No neurologic deficit.

**Assessment:**
1. Sports preparticipation examination: no cardiovascular, neurologic, or musculoskeletal contraindication to soccer.
2. Exercise-induced asthma/bronchoconstriction, currently mild and responsive to pre-exercise short-acting bronchodilator; inconsistent access and technique are modifiable risks. No current evidence of persistent uncontrolled asthma.
3. Seasonal allergic rhinitis, stable.

**Plan:**
- Cleared for soccer without restriction provided rescue medication is immediately available and the asthma action plan is followed. Completed school form and action plan.
- Renew albuterol 90 mcg inhaler: 2 puffs with spacer 15 minutes before vigorous exercise; may use every 4 hours as needed for wheeze. Demonstrated spacer technique, one puff at a time with slow inhalation, breath hold, and interval between puffs. Keep inhaler out of extreme heat and check dose counter monthly.
- Stop activity for chest tightness, cough, or wheeze. Call 911 for difficulty speaking, retractions, blue/gray lips, faintness, or poor response to rescue medication.
- Contact clinic for symptoms despite pretreatment, nighttime cough, or rescue use more than twice weekly outside planned pre-exercise dosing; consider spirometry and controller therapy if pattern worsens.
- Gradual warm-up, hydration, regular meals, adequate sleep, protective equipment, and sun protection reviewed.
- Immunizations current; influenza vaccine this fall and seasonal COVID vaccination advised.
- Follow up for asthma in 3 months or sooner for increasing symptoms.

Visit summary

What we discussed
• Sports participation and injury prevention
• Exercise-induced asthma
• Correct rescue-inhaler and spacer use
• Seasonal allergies

Next steps
