metadata.visit_title: Plaque psoriasis follow-up with biologic safety monitoring

dosageInstruction.text: Inject 150 mg subcutaneously every 12 weeks

DiagnosticReport.conclusion: CBC and liver enzymes within reference range; tuberculosis screen negative

CarePlan.title: Psoriasis control and biologic monitoring

transcript:
MA: Nisha, I have your medication list. When was your last risankizumab injection?
PT: June twelfth, at home. No trouble with the injection.
MA: Your skin questionnaire score is two. Dr. Chen will review your labs and examine the remaining spots.
DR: Hi, Nisha. How has your skin been since our winter visit?
PT: Honestly, dramatically better. My scalp is clear, and I can wear dark shirts again. I have two stubborn patches on my elbows and a tiny one behind my left ear.
DR: Any itching, cracking, bleeding, or pain?
PT: The elbows itch maybe twice a week. No bleeding. I use triamcinolone for a few days when they get rough.
DR: How much surface area do you think is involved compared with before treatment?
PT: Before, it was scalp, back, knees, elbows, and under my breasts. Now it feels like almost nothing.
DR: On examination, total involved body surface area is about one percent, with thin pink plaques on both elbows and a small postauricular plaque. Physician global assessment is one, nearly clear. No inverse plaques and no nail pitting.
PT: That is encouraging.
DR: Any joint pain with morning stiffness over thirty minutes, swollen fingers or toes, heel pain, or a whole digit swelling like a sausage?
PT: My hands are stiff for five minutes when I wake up, then fine. No swelling or heel pain.
DR: That brief stiffness is not strongly suggestive of inflammatory arthritis, but tell us if it becomes prolonged, swollen, or function-limiting. Now biologic safety: any fever, persistent cough, shortness of breath, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, recurrent infection, shingles, or infection needing antibiotics?
PT: No. I had a two-day scratchy throat after my son had a cold, but no fever and it passed.
DR: Any injection-site redness lasting more than a day, hives, facial swelling, or breathing difficulty?
PT: Just a small tender dot for an hour.
DR: Your June labs are reassuring. Blood counts and liver enzymes are within range, and tuberculosis screening is negative. Any new travel, incarceration exposure, shelter work, health-care exposure, or close contact with someone known to have tuberculosis?
PT: No. I traveled to Toronto for work, nothing higher risk that I know of.
DR: Have you received any live vaccines or been told you need one?
PT: My pharmacy asked about shingles vaccine. I was unsure because of the biologic.
DR: The recombinant shingles vaccine is not live and can be given during biologic therapy. Live vaccines should generally be avoided while receiving risankizumab unless we coordinate a safe interruption with your prescriber. Inactivated influenza and updated COVID vaccination are also appropriate.
PT: My insurance authorization expires in September. I am worried about missing a dose.
DR: We will start renewal now. Keep the specialty pharmacy messages and contact us if shipment is not scheduled two weeks before your September dose. Do not stretch doses on your own.
PT: Is it safe to stay on this for years?
DR: Long-term therapy is common when it remains effective and tolerated. We continuously balance control against infection and other risks, review screening, and update monitoring. Stopping often allows psoriasis to return. Today your response and safety data support continuing.
PT: Do I need blood tests every three months?
DR: Not necessarily. Monitoring is individualized. We will repeat CBC and liver enzymes annually or sooner if symptoms or other medicines warrant. TB risk is reviewed at each visit; repeat testing may be annual based on clinic protocol or sooner after exposure. Your current screen is negative.
PT: If I get sick near dose day, what do I do?
DR: For a mild cold without fever, call if unsure but a delay may not be necessary. For fever, significant infection, antibiotics, or a planned surgery, contact us before injecting. Do not make a permanent change yourself. Seek urgent care for breathing difficulty, facial swelling, severe widespread rash, or signs of serious infection.
PT: What should I use on the elbow patches?
DR: Triamcinolone 0.1 percent ointment in a thin layer twice daily for up to two weeks during a flare, then stop. Avoid face, groin, and skin folds. Overuse can thin skin. For the small area behind the ear, use tacrolimus ointment twice daily as needed rather than the stronger steroid; it may sting initially. Continue fragrance-free moisturizer daily.
DR: Your DLQI of two means psoriasis has a small current effect on daily life, down from 16 before treatment. That matches the examination. We will continue risankizumab 150 milligrams every twelve weeks, begin authorization renewal, and see you in six months.
PT: So next injection in early September, topical treatment only on the small spots, and call before injecting if I have fever or a significant infection.
DR: Correct. Also contact us for new prolonged joint stiffness or swelling.
PT: Thank you. This is the first summer in years I have not planned clothes around my skin.
DR: That is an important treatment outcome. We will work to keep the therapy uninterrupted and safe.
note:
**Subjective:** Nisha Patel is a 39-year-old woman with chronic plaque psoriasis on risankizumab 150 mg every 12 weeks. Last injection was June 12, administered correctly at home. She reports marked sustained improvement with only mildly pruritic elbow plaques and a small left postauricular spot. Triamcinolone is used briefly during flares. No cracking, bleeding, significant pain, injection reaction, recurrent infection, fever, persistent cough, night sweats, weight loss, shingles, or recent antibiotics. Brief morning hand stiffness lasts about five minutes without swollen joints, dactylitis, or heel pain. No new tuberculosis risk exposure. She may consider pregnancy next year. Insurance authorization expires in September.

**Objective:** Approximately 1% body surface area involved. Thin pink plaques on bilateral elbows and small left postauricular plaque; scalp clear, no inverse disease or nail pitting. Physician global assessment 1, nearly clear. DLQI 2, improved from pretreatment 16. June CBC and hepatic enzymes are within reference ranges; TB screen negative.

**Assessment:** Plaque psoriasis with excellent response and minimal residual disease on risankizumab. Biologic is tolerated without current infectious or laboratory safety concern. No convincing symptoms of psoriatic arthritis. Long-term immunomodulator monitoring and authorization renewal are due.

**Plan:** Continue risankizumab-rzaa 150 mg subcutaneously every 12 weeks; do not stretch or stop doses independently. Begin prior-authorization renewal now and contact clinic if September shipment is not arranged two weeks before dose. Continue correct refrigerated, light-protected storage; do not freeze or shake; inspect solution, rotate sites, and use sharps container. Contact clinic before dosing with fever, significant infection, antibiotic treatment, or planned surgery. Seek urgent care for breathing difficulty, facial swelling, severe widespread rash, or serious infection signs. For elbow flares, triamcinolone 0.1% ointment thinly twice daily up to 2 weeks, avoiding face/folds; use tacrolimus ointment twice daily as needed behind ear. Moisturize daily and use broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher. Avoid live vaccines during therapy unless coordinated; non-live influenza, COVID, and recombinant shingles vaccines are acceptable. Repeat CBC/liver enzymes in about one year or sooner if indicated; reassess TB risk each visit. Report prolonged morning stiffness, joint swelling, dactylitis, or heel pain. Discuss medication and pregnancy planning with dermatology and obstetrics before conception. Follow up in six months.
after_visit_summary: Continue risankizumab 150 mg every 12 weeks; we will renew authorization before September. Call before a dose if you have fever, a significant infection, antibiotics, or planned surgery. Use triamcinolone briefly on elbow flares and tacrolimus behind the ear. Avoid live vaccines, protect skin from sun, and report new prolonged joint stiffness or swelling.

metadata.visit_title: Geriatric fall-risk and polypharmacy review — orthostasis and medication simplification

code.text: Standing blood pressure at three minutes
Standing heart rate at three minutes

dosageInstruction.text: Take 1 tablet by mouth every morning; reduced from 20 mg

coding.display: Oxybutynin chloride 10 MG Extended Release Oral Tablet

statusReason.text: Anticholinergic burden, dry mouth, constipation, and fall risk
Sedation, anticholinergic burden, and fall risk

code.text: Falls prevention and home safety counseling

transcript:
DR: Mrs. Thompson, I am glad you came in. I also see your daughter is here. Is it okay if we discuss everything together?
PT: Yes. Linda keeps better notes than I do, but I still make my own decisions.
FAMILY: Absolutely. I am here because Mom asked me.
DR: Perfect. Ruth, what matters most to you today?
PT: I want people to stop acting like one fall means I cannot live at home. I want to stay in my house.
DR: Staying safely at home is our shared goal. Linda, what prompted the appointment?
FAMILY: She has fallen twice in six weeks and had another near fall. Last Tuesday she stood up after breakfast, got dizzy, and grabbed the counter.
PT: I did not fall that time.
DR: Correct, and the near fall still gives us useful information. Tell me about the two actual falls.
PT: The first was in the garden. I turned too quickly with the hose and landed on the grass. The second was at night on the way to the bathroom. My slipper caught the rug.
DR: Did you black out or lose awareness before either fall?
PT: No. I remember both. No chest pain or racing heart.
FAMILY: She had a bruise on her hip but refused the emergency room.
PT: I could walk, and the bruise faded. I did not hit my head.
DR: Any ongoing hip or groin pain now?
PT: No. My knees ache like always, but nothing new.
DR: When you feel dizzy after standing, does the room spin, or do you feel lightheaded and dim?
PT: Lightheaded, like the picture narrows for a few seconds.
DR: Our measurements today support that. Lying down, your blood pressure was 146 over 72 with pulse 68. After standing three minutes it was 118 over 64 with pulse 82, and you reported the same lightheaded feeling. That is orthostatic hypotension.
PT: Is that just old age?
DR: It becomes more common with age, but medications, hydration, and conditioning can contribute, and several of those are changeable.
FAMILY: I brought every bottle from her kitchen, including the over-the-counter ones.
DR: Excellent. Let us compare them with the chart. Ruth, tell me how you use each one.
PT: Lisinopril, the big white pill, every morning. The water pill every morning. Oxybutynin at night for my bladder. Gabapentin, one capsule at bedtime for burning feet. Tylenol when my knees complain.
FAMILY: And the blue sleep tablets.
PT: Those are just allergy pills. The bottle says diphenhydramine. I take one if I cannot sleep, maybe four nights a week.
DR: Thank you. Diphenhydramine can cause sedation, confusion, blurred vision, constipation, and falls in older adults. Oxybutynin has similar anticholinergic effects. Together they create a substantial medication burden.
PT: The bladder pill does not work very well anyway. My mouth is dry all the time.
FAMILY: She is also constipated.
PT: Sometimes. We do not need to announce every detail.
DR: Those details help us connect symptoms to treatment, but you control what we discuss. Would you be willing to stop diphenhydramine completely?
PT: If you give me another way to sleep.
DR: We can use a non-drug sleep plan: consistent wake time, daylight and activity during the day, no naps after 2 p.m., and a quiet wind-down routine. Melatonin can still cause grogginess, so I would first see how you do without the antihistamine.
PT: I watch the eleven o'clock news in bed. It does not exactly calm me down.
FAMILY: We have been telling her that.
DR: Perhaps news in the living room and something quieter in the bedroom. Ruth, does that sound acceptable?
PT: I can try it for two weeks.
DR: I also recommend stopping oxybutynin because of dry mouth, constipation, memory, and fall concerns. We can treat urgency with scheduled bathroom trips every two to three hours while awake, limiting evening fluids without becoming dehydrated, and pelvic-floor therapy.
PT: If I stop it, am I going to have accidents?
DR: Urgency may temporarily increase. Keep a three-day bladder diary. If behavioral treatment is insufficient, we can consider a lower-risk medicine after checking blood pressure and cost.
FAMILY: She rushes to the bathroom at night, which is when she fell.
DR: A bedside commode temporarily or a clear, well-lit route could reduce rushing.
PT: I do not want a commode in my bedroom. A night-light and clearing the rug are fine.
DR: That is your choice. We will document the option and start with what you accept.
PT: What about the blood pressure pills? My home readings are often around 125.
DR: The hydrochlorothiazide water pill can reduce circulating volume and worsen urinary urgency. I recommend stopping hydrochlorothiazide 25 milligrams today and reducing lisinopril from 20 to 10 milligrams each morning.
FAMILY: Will her pressure get dangerously high?
DR: We will monitor rather than guess. Check seated blood pressure in the morning and again when symptomatic, and bring the log. Call if repeated readings are above 170 over 100 or below 100 systolic with symptoms. We will recheck here in two weeks.
PT: You are taking away three medicines at once. How will we know which one helped?
DR: That is a fair question. Diphenhydramine poses immediate nighttime fall risk, hydrochlorothiazide contributes to the measured pressure drop and urgency, and oxybutynin adds anticholinergic effects without much benefit. Each has a distinct reason to stop, and we can follow sleep, bladder symptoms, blood pressure, and dizziness separately. If you prefer, oxybutynin can stop after three days rather than today.
PT: Three days makes me more comfortable.
DR: Agreed. Stop diphenhydramine and hydrochlorothiazide today, reduce lisinopril tomorrow, and stop oxybutynin on Sunday. Linda, can you help update the pillbox with Ruth's permission?
PT: Yes, but I want to watch.
FAMILY: Of course. We will do it together.
DR: The gabapentin may also contribute to unsteadiness. Does it clearly help the burning feet?
PT: I think so. When I miss it, my toes burn more.
DR: Since it has clear benefit and the dose is modest, we will leave 300 milligrams at bedtime unchanged today. If falls continue after the first changes, we can reassess it rather than changing everything.
FAMILY: That makes sense.
DR: How much fluid do you drink?
PT: Two cups of coffee and maybe three glasses of water. I avoid drinking because of the bladder.
DR: That may worsen orthostasis. Unless another clinician has restricted fluids, aim for about six cups of nonalcoholic fluid spread through the day, with less during the two hours before bed. Rise in stages: sit on the bed edge, pump your ankles, then stand holding something stable.
PT: I can do that.
DR: We timed your walking today. The Timed Up and Go was 16.8 seconds, which indicates increased fall risk. You use a cane outside but not inside?
PT: Correct. The cane gets in my way in the kitchen.
DR: Physical therapy can assess strength, balance, and the safest device. Would you accept home physical therapy for the first few visits?
PT: Home visits would be convenient.
FAMILY: And they can see the stairs.
DR: Exactly. I will order home health physical therapy and a home safety evaluation. They can look at grab bars, lighting, footwear, and the loose rugs.
PT: The hallway rug belonged to my mother. I am not throwing it away.
DR: Could it be secured with a non-slip backing or moved to a wall?
PT: We can hang it. That is better than removing it from the house.
FAMILY: I can arrange that this weekend.
DR: Good compromise. Do you have grab bars in the shower?
PT: One suction handle.
DR: Suction handles can release unexpectedly. A professionally mounted grab bar and non-slip shower surface are safer.
FAMILY: I will call the handyman.
DR: Ruth, we also did a brief memory screen. You scored three out of five, which is borderline and similar to last year's result. You manage basic activities independently, but Linda fills the pillbox weekly. Any stove left on, bills missed, or getting lost?
PT: No getting lost. I paid the electric bill twice in May. That was annoying, not disastrous.
FAMILY: She told me right away, and we set up alerts.
DR: That sounds like mild cognitive difficulty with good compensation, not an immediate reason to change where you live. Removing anticholinergic medicines may help attention. We will repeat cognitive assessment after medication changes and check hearing, vision, B12, and thyroid status if not current.
PT: Thank you for not talking over me.
DR: You are the patient and the decision-maker. Linda's observations add information, but the plan needs your agreement.
PT: I agree to the medication changes, home therapy, and fixing the rugs and bathroom bar.
DR: Excellent. Continue acetaminophen for knee pain, up to 1,000 milligrams twice daily as needed, maximum 3,000 milligrams from all sources. Avoid ibuprofen unless your clinician advises it because of kidney and blood pressure risks.
PT: I only use Tylenol.
DR: Before we finish, what would require urgent care? A fall with a head strike, loss of consciousness, new weakness, inability to bear weight, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or persistent confusion. Call our clinic for worsening dizziness or another fall even without injury.
FAMILY: We will keep the phone in her pocket, not on the kitchen charger.
PT: I can manage that.
DR: We will call in three business days to review the transition and see you in two weeks for orthostatic vitals and the blood pressure log. Bring every medication again.
PT: All right. The goal is still my house.
DR: Yes. These changes are specifically designed to support that goal safely.
note:
**Subjective:** Ruth Thompson is an 88-year-old independently living woman accompanied, with permission, by her daughter Linda for evaluation of two falls and one near fall over six weeks. She explicitly prioritizes remaining in her own home and retains decision-making authority. One fall occurred while turning in the garden and one at night when a slipper caught a hallway rug en route to the bathroom. She denies loss of consciousness, head strike, chest pain, palpitations, or persistent injury. She describes brief visual dimming/lightheadedness after standing, without vertigo. Medication reconciliation using bottles brought from home identified lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, oxybutynin ER 10 mg nightly, gabapentin 300 mg nightly, acetaminophen as needed, and nonprescription diphenhydramine 25 mg approximately four nights weekly for sleep. Oxybutynin provides limited benefit and is associated with dry mouth and constipation. She limits water because of urinary urgency. Gabapentin clearly reduces burning foot pain. Daughter fills the weekly pillbox with patient participation. Patient denies getting lost or stove-safety events but reports one duplicated utility payment; compensatory alerts are in place.

**Objective:** Supine BP 146/72 mmHg and pulse 68; after three minutes standing, BP 118/64 and pulse 82 with reproduced lightheadedness. Timed Up and Go is 16.8 seconds, consistent with increased fall risk. Gait is cautious; she uses a cane outdoors. No focal neurologic deficit or acute hip tenderness. Mini-Cog score is 3/5, borderline and reportedly stable from last year. Medication review demonstrates combined sedative, anticholinergic, antihypertensive, and diuretic burden.

**Assessment:**
1. Multifactorial recurrent falls and near fall related to symptomatic orthostatic hypotension, high-risk medications, nocturnal urinary urgency, environmental hazards, and impaired mobility. No syncope or current injury.
2. Orthostatic hypotension with 28-mmHg systolic drop, likely exacerbated by hydrochlorothiazide, lisinopril intensity, and low fluid intake.
3. Polypharmacy with anticholinergic burden from diphenhydramine and oxybutynin; associated dry mouth, constipation, possible cognitive effects, and fall risk.
4. Urge incontinence with limited oxybutynin response.
5. Mild cognitive impairment with preserved basic independence and effective family supports.
6. Chronic neuropathic foot pain and knee osteoarthritis.

**Plan:** Stop diphenhydramine today and use a nonpharmacologic sleep plan with consistent wake time, daytime light/activity, no naps after 2 p.m., and a quiet screen-free wind-down routine. Stop hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg today. Reduce lisinopril from 20 mg to 10 mg each morning beginning tomorrow. By shared decision, stop oxybutynin ER 10 mg on 07/05/2026 after a three-day transition; begin scheduled voiding every 2–3 hours while awake, three-day bladder diary, and pelvic-floor therapy referral. Continue gabapentin 300 mg nightly unchanged because of clear benefit; reassess if falls persist. Encourage approximately six cups of nonalcoholic fluid spread through the day unless otherwise restricted, with reduced intake for two hours before bed. Rise in stages and perform ankle pumps before standing. Record seated home BP each morning and when symptomatic; call for repeated BP above 170/100 or symptomatic systolic BP below 100. Home health physical therapy and home safety evaluation ordered for gait, balance, assistive-device assessment, mounted shower grab bar, lighting, footwear, and rug securing/removal. Patient and daughter will update the pillbox together. Continue acetaminophen up to 1,000 mg twice daily as needed, maximum 3,000 mg/day from all sources. Clinic will call in three business days; follow up in two weeks with medication bottles, BP log, and repeat orthostatic vitals. Repeat cognitive assessment after deprescribing and confirm vision, hearing, B12, and thyroid evaluation. Seek urgent care for fall with head strike, loss of consciousness, new focal weakness, inability to bear weight, chest pain, severe dyspnea, or persistent confusion; report any additional fall or worsening dizziness promptly.
after_visit_summary:
Visit summary

What we discussed
• Two falls and one near fall are likely related to orthostatic blood-pressure drop, medication effects, urinary urgency, and home hazards.
• Blood pressure changed from 146/72 lying down to 118/64 after standing 3 minutes, with lightheadedness.
• Diphenhydramine and oxybutynin add sedation and anticholinergic effects that can worsen falls, dry mouth, constipation, and attention.

Next steps
• Stop diphenhydramine and hydrochlorothiazide today.
• Reduce lisinopril from 20 mg to 10 mg every morning beginning tomorrow.
• Stop oxybutynin ER 10 mg on 07/05/2026. Use scheduled bathroom trips every 2–3 hours while awake and keep a 3-day bladder diary.
• Continue gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime for now.
• Drink about 6 cups of nonalcoholic fluid through the day unless another clinician has restricted fluids; reduce fluids for 2 hours before bed. Sit first, pump your ankles, and stand slowly while holding a stable surface.
• Record seated blood pressure every morning and when dizzy. Call for repeated readings above 170/100 or symptomatic top number below 100.
• Home physical therapy and a home safety evaluation were ordered. Secure or relocate loose rugs, improve night lighting, and install a mounted shower grab bar.
• Clinic will call in 3 business days. Return in 2 weeks with all medication bottles and the blood-pressure log.
• Seek urgent care after a fall with head strike, loss of consciousness, new weakness, inability to bear weight, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or persistent confusion. Report another fall or worsening dizziness promptly.

metadata.visit_title: Family goals-of-care visit for metastatic lung cancer

reasonCode.text: Clarify goals and treatment preferences after cancer progression

CarePlan.title: Comfort-focused home care and hospice referral

detail.description: Hospice informational visit and home symptom management

category.text: Do-not-resuscitate and do-not-intubate preference documented after informed discussion

transcript:
Dr. Raman: Mrs. Sato, thank you for welcoming me into your home. Emi is here, and the Japanese interpreter is on video. Is it all right to discuss the scan and future care together?

Patient: Yes. Emi should hear everything. Please speak plainly.

Daughter: I want Mom to decide. I may ask questions, but it is her choice.

Dr. Raman: That is helpful. Before I explain, what have you understood from Dr. Chen?

Patient: The cancer grew in my liver and bones even after the second medicine. Another chemotherapy might slow it, but it could make me weaker. I am already tired.

Dr. Raman: That is accurate. The oncology team estimates another treatment has a small chance of shrinking the cancer and a substantial chance of fatigue, infection, nausea, and more clinic time. Without more cancer-directed treatment, time may be measured in a few months, though no one can predict an exact day. With treatment, it may or may not be longer. I wish the choices were better.

Patient: A few months is not surprising. I can feel my body changing.

Daughter: Is she giving up if she says no?

Dr. Raman: No. Choosing how to use limited time is active medical decision-making. We can treat pain, breathlessness, anxiety, constipation, and nausea whether or not she receives chemotherapy. Mrs. Sato, what matters most if time may be short?

Patient: Being home. Sitting in the garden. Seeing my grandson graduate from middle school if I can. I do not want my days spent in the emergency room. I want to recognize my family and talk with them.

Dr. Raman: What are you most worried about?

Patient: Suffocating, and being a burden to Emi. Also pain. The morphine helps, but I wait too long because I fear it means the end.

Dr. Raman: Morphine used carefully for pain and breathlessness does not mean you are surrendering. Your current low dose is intended to help you breathe and move more comfortably. We will pair it with senna because constipation is predictable. Emi, what worries you?

Daughter: Missing an emergency I should have fixed. Last Sunday she was gasping after the bathroom, and I almost called 911. She recovered after the morphine, but I did not know whether I had done the right thing.

Dr. Raman: That uncertainty is exhausting. Hospice provides a nurse line day and night, home visits, medicines and equipment related to comfort, and guidance during changes. It is generally for people thought likely to have six months or less if illness follows its usual course.

Patient: I want the visit. I do not want more chemotherapy.

Daughter: I support that. I am sad, but I heard you.

Dr. Raman: Let us also discuss emergency treatments. If your heart stopped, CPR would involve hard chest compressions, shocks in some cases, and likely hospitalization. With advanced cancer and your current weakness, it would be very unlikely to restore the kind of life you described and could cause injury. If breathing failed, a breathing tube and ventilator would usually mean intensive care and might not lead back home. What would you want?

Patient: No chest compressions and no breathing machine. Keep me comfortable.

Dr. Raman: To confirm, you prefer do not resuscitate and do not intubate, while continuing treatments that support comfort at home.

Patient: Correct.

Dr. Raman: Who should speak for you if illness makes you unable to communicate?

Patient: Emi. My son Ken agrees; we discussed it.

Dr. Raman: We will document Emi as the surrogate and complete the portable medical order with your oncology team. Please keep a copy where emergency personnel can find it. Today your breathlessness is three out of ten at rest and worse with walking. How are pain, nausea, bowels, and appetite?

Patient: Right hip pain is four, down to one after morphine. Mild nausea in the morning. I eat small bowls of soup. No bowel movement for three days.

Dr. Raman: Take senna two tablets tonight and then nightly; add a morning dose if there is no bowel movement by tomorrow. Continue morphine solution at the prescribed dose every four hours as needed for pain or shortness of breath; call before increasing it. Use the fan toward your face, rest before activity, and keep the bedside commode nearby. Continue ondansetron as prescribed for nausea.

Daughter: When should I call hospice versus 911?

Dr. Raman: Once enrolled, call hospice first for expected worsening pain, breathlessness, confusion, falls, fever, or inability to take medicines. Call 911 if your mother asks for emergency transport or for an unexpected situation outside the comfort plan. Until enrollment, call our palliative line for symptoms and 911 for severe distress you cannot manage.

Patient: I feel calmer knowing there will be someone to call.

Patient: No. I want tea in my garden this afternoon.

Daughter: We can do that.

Dr. Raman: Then that is today’s priority.
note:
PALLIATIVE CARE GOALS-OF-CARE NOTE

Participants: Haruko Sato, daughter Emi Sato, Dr. Priya Raman, and certified Japanese video interpreter. Patient gave permission for shared discussion and demonstrated decision-making capacity.

Clinical context: Seventy-nine-year-old woman with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer involving liver and bone, progressive after second-line systemic therapy. Oncology has offered another regimen with low likelihood of response and meaningful toxicity risk. Prognosis was discussed as likely months without precision. Functional status is declining; Palliative Performance Scale is 50%. Dyspnea is 3/10 at rest and worse with exertion. Right hip pain improves from 4/10 to 1/10 with prescribed morphine. Mild morning nausea, reduced intake, and constipation for three days are present.

Understanding and values: Patient accurately understands cancer progression and treatment tradeoffs. She prioritizes remaining at home, comfort, mental clarity, time with family, her garden, and possibly attending her grandson’s graduation. She wishes to avoid emergency-department and intensive-care time and fears suffocation, uncontrolled pain, and burdening her daughter.

Decisions: After discussion of benefits and burdens, patient declines further cancer-directed chemotherapy and requests a hospice informational visit with intent toward comfort-focused home care. She chooses do-not-resuscitate and do-not-intubate status. She wants ongoing symptom-directed treatment but no chest compressions or mechanical ventilation if dying. She identifies daughter Emi as surrogate if capacity is lost; patient states son Ken is aware and agrees. Daughter expressed sadness, asked clarifying questions, and affirmed support.

Assessment: Preferences are informed, internally consistent, and aligned with stated goals. No coercion identified. Patient and family would benefit from hospice access and explicit crisis guidance.

Plan: Refer for hospice informational visit within 48 hours. Coordinate portable medical orders documenting DNR/DNI with oncology and send preferences to oncology and primary care. Continue prescribed morphine oral solution every four hours as needed for pain or dyspnea; call before dose escalation. Use fan, activity pacing, and bedside commode. Take senna two tablets tonight and nightly; add morning dose if no bowel movement by tomorrow. Continue prescribed ondansetron for nausea. Palliative nurse will call tomorrow regarding breathing and constipation. After hospice enrollment, call hospice first for expected symptom changes; before enrollment, call palliative care for guidance and 911 for severe unmanageable distress or if patient requests emergency transport.
after_visit_summary: You chose comfort-focused care at home, declined further chemotherapy, and requested a hospice informational visit within 48 hours. Your preference is do not resuscitate and do not intubate, with Emi as surrogate; these decisions will be shared with oncology and primary care. Continue prescribed morphine as needed for pain or breathlessness and call before increasing it. Start senna tonight, continue ondansetron as prescribed, and expect a nurse call tomorrow. Call the hospice or palliative line first for expected symptom changes; use 911 for severe unmanageable distress or if you request emergency transport.

metadata.visit_title: COPD follow-up, inhaler technique, and smoking cessation

Observation.valueString: 128/76 mmHg

dosageInstruction.text: Inhale two puffs once daily
Apply one patch daily

CarePlan.title: COPD and tobacco cessation plan

transcript:
NURSE: Teresa, your blood pressure is 128 over 76, breathing rate 18, and oxygen level 95 percent on room air. Your COPD questionnaire score is 14.
PT: That is a little better than last time, right?
NURSE: Last time was 17. Jordan will review the details.
NP: Good afternoon. Since our visit three months ago, have you needed urgent care, prednisone, antibiotics, or the emergency department for breathing?
PT: No. I had one bad cold but rode it out at home.
NP: Any increase in cough, sputum amount, or change to yellow, green, or bloody mucus?
PT: I cough most mornings and bring up clear stuff. Nothing bloody and no recent change.
NP: How far can you walk before stopping?
PT: On flat ground about three blocks. Hills still get me. I stop halfway up the stairs at my daughter's apartment.
NP: Any shortness of breath at rest, waking breathless, chest pain, fainting, leg swelling, fever, or unplanned weight loss?
PT: No. I sleep on one pillow. My ankles look normal.
NP: How often are you using albuterol?
PT: Maybe four times a week, usually before errands.
NP: And the tiotropium-olodaterol, two inhalations every day?
PT: Most days. I miss Sunday sometimes because the routine changes. I am not certain I am doing the twist correctly.
NP: Please show me with your inhaler.
PT: I turn it, open it, and breathe in fast like this.
NP: I see two fixable points. First breathe out fully away from the device. Seal your lips around the mouthpiece without covering the vents. Then take a slow, deep breath while pressing the dose button, keep inhaling, and hold for about ten seconds. Let us reset and try again.
PT: Slow instead of fast. That feels different.
NP: Good seal and better breath. Repeat once because your dose is two inhalations. Do not spray toward the eyes. How do you remember weekdays?
PT: It sits by the coffee maker. Sunday I go to church before coffee.
NP: Could you set a daily phone alarm and keep it beside your toothbrush instead?
PT: The alarm would work.
NP: Your symptoms are moderate but stable, with no exacerbations since the last visit. Correct daily controller use may reduce rescue use. We will continue the same inhaler rather than escalate today.
PT: I was worried you would add steroids.
NP: There is no indication for oral steroids now. An inhaled steroid is not automatically helpful for every COPD patient and can increase pneumonia risk. We would reconsider based on exacerbations and other features.
NP: How many cigarettes are you smoking?
PT: About twelve a day. It was a pack. The first one is within fifteen minutes of waking.
NP: You have already reduced, which tells us you can change the pattern. On a scale from zero to ten, how ready are you to stop completely?
PT: Seven. My granddaughter asks why I smell like smoke. I also get nervous because cigarettes calm me down.
NP: What would move seven to eight?
PT: A plan that does not make me miserable at work. I tried gum alone and chewed it like regular gum. I got hiccups and quit using it.
NP: Combination nicotine replacement can help: a steady patch plus gum for breakthrough cravings. Because you smoke more than ten daily and light up soon after waking, start a 21-milligram patch each morning. Rotate sites and remove the old patch. If vivid dreams occur, remove it at bedtime. For cravings, use 4-milligram gum: chew slowly until peppery, park between cheek and gum, then repeat for about thirty minutes. Avoid food and acidic drinks for fifteen minutes before and during use.
PT: Can I smoke while wearing it?
NP: The goal is no cigarettes starting on your quit date. A slip is not a reason to abandon treatment, but continued smoking while using nicotine can cause nausea, dizziness, palpitations, or headache. Stop smoking and call if those occur; seek urgent care for severe chest symptoms.
PT: What date should I choose?
NP: You mentioned your granddaughter visits July fifth. Would July first give you a clear start and several days before that visit?
PT: July first. I can throw out the ashtrays the night before.
NP: Excellent. Ask your daughter not to smoke around you, tell coworkers you are quitting, and plan a five-minute walk after lunch instead of the smoking area. Our quitline offers coaching.
PT: I would take a phone call after six.
NP: I will send the referral with that preference.
NP: Review your action signs: if breathlessness, cough, or sputum rises beyond usual, call early. Go urgently for severe breathlessness at rest, blue lips, confusion, fainting, or chest pressure.
PT: Daily controller with the slow breath, albuterol only as needed, patch and gum starting July first, quitline call, and CT in August.
NP: Exactly. We will check by phone one week after your quit date and see you in three months.
note:
**Subjective:** Teresa Ramirez is a 68-year-old woman with COPD and active tobacco use returning for three-month follow-up. She reports stable morning cough with clear sputum and exertional dyspnea after approximately three flat blocks or halfway up stairs. No dyspnea at rest, nocturnal breathlessness, chest pain, syncope, edema, fever, hemoptysis, weight loss, or sputum change. She has had no interval emergency visits, antibiotics, prednisone, or COPD exacerbations. Albuterol is used about four times weekly. Tiotropium-olodaterol is taken most days, with occasional Sunday omission and uncertainty about technique. She smokes about 12 cigarettes daily, down from 20, with first cigarette within 15 minutes of waking. Readiness to quit is 7/10. Prior gum use caused hiccups because she chewed continuously.

**Objective:** BP 128/76 mmHg, RR 18/min, resting SpO2 95% on room air. CAT score 14, improved from 17. Comfortable conversation, no accessory-muscle use. Demonstrated rapid inhalation without prior exhalation; technique corrected successfully with teach-back.

**Assessment:** COPD with moderate stable symptoms and no recent exacerbation. Controller adherence and delivery technique can improve. No current indication for systemic steroids, home oxygen, or regimen escalation. Nicotine dependence with high morning dependence; motivated for a planned quit attempt. Remains eligible for annual lung cancer screening.

**Plan:** Continue tiotropium-olodaterol two inhalations daily and albuterol as needed. Use daily alarm; exhale away from device, seal lips, inhale slowly and deeply during actuation, hold approximately 10 seconds, and repeat. Repeat spirometry before three-month follow-up. Quit date July 1. Start nicotine 21 mg patch daily, rotating sites; remove at bedtime if vivid dreams. Add nicotine 4 mg gum for cravings using chew-and-park technique; avoid food or acidic drinks around dosing. Reviewed excess nicotine symptoms and urgent chest precautions. Refer to state quitline with evening-call preference; telephone follow-up one week after quit date. Remove tobacco cues and substitute a brief post-lunch walk. Order annual low-dose chest CT for August after discussion of benefits and false-positive findings. Influenza vaccination this fall; pneumococcal status current. Call early for increased dyspnea, cough, or sputum. Seek urgent care for severe resting breathlessness, cyanosis, confusion, syncope, or chest pressure.
after_visit_summary: Continue the daily controller inhaler with the slow-deep-breath technique; use albuterol as needed. Quit date is July 1: start the 21 mg patch and use 4 mg chew-and-park gum for cravings. Quitline will call after 6 PM. CT screening is planned for August. Get urgent help for severe breathlessness, blue lips, confusion, fainting, or chest pressure.

metadata.visit_title: Type 2 diabetes follow-up — glycemic control and new foot paresthesias

reasonCode.text: Type 2 diabetes and burning feet

code.text: Distal symmetric sensory neuropathy, suspected diabetic

dosageInstruction.text: Take 2 tablets (1000 mg) by mouth with the evening meal
Take 1 tablet by mouth each morning

transcript:
MA: Good morning, Mr. Okafor. I have 132 over 78 for blood pressure and 96.4 kilograms for weight. Did you bring your medication bottles?
PT: I brought the whole plastic bag. My wife said if I forgot it again, she would deliver it herself.
MA: Excellent motivation. I will let Dr. Reed know about the burning sensation you wrote on the intake form.
DR: Chinedu, good to see you. I reviewed the labs. Before we get into numbers, how have you been taking the medicines?
PT: Metformin, two of the 500 extended-release tablets with dinner. Losartan and atorvastatin at night. The empagliflozin in the morning, except I ran out about five weeks ago.
DR: What got in the way of refilling it?
PT: The pharmacy said the copay was ninety dollars after my insurance changed. I thought I could manage with the metformin until this appointment.
DR: Thank you for saying that. Cost changes the plan. Any missed metformin?
PT: Maybe one evening a week when my delivery route ends late. It does not upset my stomach.
DR: Your A1c is 8.4 percent, up from 7.3 six months ago. The gap in empagliflozin and some missed doses likely contribute. What have home sugars shown?
PT: Fasting is usually 160 to 190. I check three mornings a week. Once it was 224 after a birthday weekend. No lows.
DR: Increased thirst, frequent urination, blurry vision, nausea, or weight loss?
PT: More thirsty when it is hot, but no major change. No blurry vision or weight loss.
DR: Tell me about the foot symptoms.
PT: For maybe two months, both soles burn at night, especially the toes. It feels like hot sand or tiny electric shocks. During the day it is mostly numbness, like thick socks even when I am barefoot.
DR: Both sides equally? Does it travel above the ankles?
PT: Right is a little worse, but both. It stays below the ankles.
DR: Any weakness, tripping, back pain shooting down a leg, or trouble controlling bladder or bowel?
PT: No weakness. No back pain. I drive a delivery van, so my back gets stiff, but nothing shoots down.
DR: Any cuts, blisters, color change, cold foot, swelling, or pain in the calves when walking?
PT: I found a small blister on the right little toe last month from new work boots. My wife cleaned it and it healed. No current sores.
DR: Alcohol use? Certain vitamin deficiencies and alcohol can also affect nerves.
PT: One or two beers on Saturday, not every week.
DR: Any vegetarian diet, stomach surgery, thyroid problems, chemotherapy, or family nerve disease?
PT: None. I eat meat. No surgery.
DR: The pattern sounds like distal symmetric neuropathy, often related to diabetes, but we should check other reversible causes. Kidney function is good: creatinine 0.92, estimated filtration 103. Urine albumin ratio is 18, which is normal. I added vitamin B12 because metformin can lower it; it is 238, at the low end of normal. We will also check TSH and serum protein testing.
PT: Does that mean the numbness will go away if the sugar improves?
DR: Better glucose control can prevent progression and sometimes improves burning, but established numbness may not fully reverse. Foot protection matters because reduced sensation can hide an injury.
MA: I can set up the monofilament and tuning fork.
DR: Please. Chinedu, shoes and socks off. I am checking skin, pulses, strength, and sensation.
PT: The floor is cold, but my toes barely notice it.
DR: Skin is intact with no ulcer. Pulses are strong. Strength and ankle reflexes are symmetric. You feel the monofilament at the heels and midfoot but miss it at three of the five toe sites on each foot. Vibration is reduced at both great toes. That supports sensory neuropathy.
PT: Is there medicine for the burning? It wakes me twice a week.
DR: There is, but your symptoms are intermittent and medicines such as gabapentin can cause sleepiness—important for a driver. I recommend we first restore diabetes treatment, start oral B12, and use non-drug measures. If pain remains disruptive, we can discuss a low bedtime dose with explicit driving precautions.
PT: I do not want anything that makes me sleepy behind the wheel.
DR: Agreed. For diabetes, our pharmacist found a manufacturer copay card that should bring empagliflozin to ten dollars if you qualify. We will send a new 10-milligram prescription. If the card fails, call us rather than going without it; we can choose a lower-cost alternative.
PT: Should I increase metformin?
DR: You are already at 1,000 milligrams nightly, and we could eventually increase, but adherence to the current dose plus restarting empagliflozin is the first step. Use a phone alarm and keep a spare evening dose in your lunch bag, protected from heat. Do not double a missed dose.
PT: What side effects should I remember for the morning pill?
DR: Empagliflozin can increase urination and genital yeast infections. Stay hydrated. Stop it and call if you cannot eat or drink because of vomiting, fever, or surgery; it can rarely cause ketoacidosis even without extremely high glucose. Seek urgent care for nausea, abdominal pain, deep breathing, or severe illness. We will give written sick-day guidance.
PT: I fast for religious holidays sometimes.
DR: Please contact us before prolonged fasting so we can plan medication and glucose checks safely.
DR: Food and schedule—what is realistic on delivery days?
PT: Breakfast is coffee and a pastry at the depot. Lunch is whatever is near the route. Dinner is home food, usually rice, stew, vegetables.
DR: Could you pack breakfast four days a week—eggs, plain yogurt, or leftovers—and choose half the usual rice portion while adding vegetables and protein?
PT: Packing breakfast is possible. My wife already packs hers.
DR: Activity?
PT: I sit most of the shift. I walk Sunday mornings.
DR: Start with a ten-minute walk after dinner five days a week and inspect your feet afterward. Check both feet daily with a mirror, including between toes. No barefoot walking, even indoors. Test bath water with your elbow, not your feet. Wear well-fitting shoes and clean dry socks, and call the same day for a blister, crack, redness, warmth, drainage, or swelling. Do not trim calluses yourself.
PT: I have been using a heating pad on the soles.
DR: Please stop direct heat; numb skin can burn without warning. A podiatry referral is appropriate for baseline care and shoe guidance.
PT: Eye exam was last summer.
DR: It is due again. We will refer for a dilated retinal exam. Continue losartan 50 and atorvastatin 20; blood pressure is acceptable and renal testing is reassuring.
PT: When do we check the A1c again?
DR: In three months. Send fasting readings through the portal in two weeks, and our pharmacist will call in one week to confirm you obtained the medication. Goal fasting is generally 80 to 130, but call for repeated readings above 300 or any symptoms of severe illness.
PT: That feels manageable. The foot part worries me more than the number.
DR: That concern is useful if it leads to daily checks, not panic. There is no ulcer or weakness today. We are acting early.
MA: I have the foot-care handout and the copay-card instructions.
DR: Great. Chinedu, repeat the plan back to me.
PT: Restart the morning empagliflozin if the card works, keep metformin two tablets with dinner, start B12, check feet every day, no heating pad, send sugars in two weeks, and come back in three months. Call sooner for any foot wound or if I get sick and cannot eat.
DR: Exactly.
note:
**Subjective:** Chinedu Okafor is a 48-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obesity presenting for medication follow-up and two months of bilateral burning and numbness in the toes and soles. Symptoms are worse at night, remain below the ankles, and wake him about twice weekly. He denies weakness, falls, radicular pain, bowel/bladder dysfunction, claudication, or current wounds. A shoe-related blister healed. He stopped empagliflozin five weeks ago after an insurance change raised the copay to $90 and misses approximately one metformin dose weekly. Fasting glucose is usually 160-190 mg/dL without hypoglycemia. No polyuria, visual change, weight loss, or systemic illness. Alcohol is minimal.

**Objective:** BP 132/78 mmHg; weight 96.4 kg. A1c 8.4% (prior 7.3%), glucose 176 mg/dL, creatinine 0.92 mg/dL, eGFR 103 mL/min/1.73m2, urine albumin/creatinine 18 mg/g, vitamin B12 238 pg/mL. Feet warm and intact without ulcer or deformity; pedal pulses strong. Monofilament sensation absent at 3/5 toe sites bilaterally with preserved heel/midfoot sensation. Vibration reduced at great toes. Strength and ankle reflexes symmetric.

**Assessment:**
1. Type 2 diabetes, above individualized goal because of medication access gap and intermittent missed doses. No nephropathy.
2. Distal symmetric sensory neuropathy, likely diabetic; low-normal B12 may contribute. No motor deficit, ulcer, vascular compromise, or red-flag spinal features.
3. Hypertension, controlled on losartan.
4. Hyperlipidemia, on statin.

**Plan:**
- Restart empagliflozin 10 mg each morning using manufacturer copay support; pharmacist call in one week. If unaffordable, patient will call for an alternative rather than stop therapy. Continue metformin ER 1,000 mg with evening meal; use adherence alarm and do not double missed doses.
- Empagliflozin adverse effects and sick-day hold reviewed. Hold during inability to eat/drink, significant febrile illness, surgery, or prolonged fasting after contacting clinic. Seek urgent care for nausea, abdominal pain, deep breathing, or severe illness.
- Start oral vitamin B12 1,000 mcg daily. Order TSH and serum protein electrophoresis to evaluate alternate neuropathy causes. Defer sedating neuropathic medication because symptoms are intermittent and patient drives professionally; reconsider if pain persists.
- Daily foot inspection with mirror, no barefoot walking or direct heat, well-fitting footwear and dry socks. Same-day call for blister, crack, redness, warmth, drainage, or swelling. Podiatry referral placed.
- Pack higher-protein breakfast, reduce rice portion, and walk 10 minutes after dinner five days weekly.
- Send fasting glucose log in 2 weeks; call for repeated values above 300 mg/dL or severe illness. Repeat A1c and visit in 3 months.
- Dilated retinal examination referral placed. Continue losartan 50 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.
after_visit_summary:
Visit summary

What we discussed
• Type 2 diabetes above goal (A1c 8.4%)
• Burning and reduced sensation in both feet
• Medication cost and adherence
• Daily diabetic foot protection

Next steps
• Restart empagliflozin 10 mg each morning using copay support; call if it remains unaffordable.
• Continue metformin ER 1,000 mg with dinner. Do not double a missed dose.
• Start vitamin B12 1,000 mcg daily; complete ordered thyroid and protein blood tests.
• Hold empagliflozin and call during inability to eat/drink, significant fever, surgery, or planned prolonged fasting.
• Check both feet daily. Do not walk barefoot or use direct heat. Call the same day for any blister, crack, redness, warmth, drainage, or swelling.
• Podiatry and dilated eye-exam referrals were placed.
• Send fasting glucose readings in 2 weeks; pharmacist will call in 1 week.
• Repeat A1c and follow up in 3 months.

metadata.visit_title: Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis

reasonCode.text: developed steady left lower abdominal pain with mild nausea

Observation.valueString: CT showed localized inflammation without abscess, obstruction, free air, or perforation

transcript:
Triage nurse: Hello, Camila. Please tell me in your own words what brought you to emergency department today.

Patient: I developed steady left lower abdominal pain with mild nausea. I was concerned it might be serious and wanted an examination. The symptoms changed enough that home care did not feel sufficient.

Triage nurse: I will document your medicines, allergies, and vital signs. Have you had fainting, severe breathing trouble, confusion, uncontrolled bleeding, or another immediate emergency symptom?

Patient: No. I have not had those problems. I can answer questions clearly, and I brought my medication list. I would like to understand what the testing means and what I should watch for at home.

Clinician: I reviewed the history, nursing assessment, medicines, allergies, and relevant prior records. On examination you are alert and appropriately interactive. Your circulation and breathing are stable. The focused examination fits the history, without a finding that requires an immediate invasive intervention.

Patient: What did the tests show? Do I need to stay in the hospital or have another procedure?

Clinician: Ct showed localized inflammation without abscess, obstruction, free air, or perforation. Taken together with your examination, the working diagnosis is acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis. Your response to care and current stability make discharge reasonable today. We discussed that tests reduce uncertainty but cannot predict every change after discharge.

Patient: What should I do first when I get home, and may I return to normal activity?

Clinician: Use a clear-liquid diet briefly, advance food as pain improves, and schedule follow-up with primary care. Start gently and increase activity only as comfort and the written restrictions allow. Do not share prescriptions, double a missed dose, or add an over-the-counter product without checking the label and possible interactions.

Patient: Please review the medicine plan. I want to make sure I heard it correctly.

Clinician: The medication plan is amoxicillin-clavulanate per shared decision. Follow the printed dose and timing. Stop and seek advice for a suspected medication reaction. Keep the follow-up appointment because improvement should be confirmed and the plan may need adjustment.

Patient: Which symptoms mean I should return right away instead of waiting for the appointment?

Clinician: Seek urgent reassessment for increasing pain, persistent fever, repeated vomiting, fainting, abdominal rigidity, or inability to hydrate. Call emergency services for severe breathing difficulty, collapse, new confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms. If you are uncertain and cannot reach the clinic, emergency evaluation is appropriate.

Triage nurse: Your written instructions and follow-up information are ready. Is there any barrier to obtaining medicine, transportation, food, help at home, or understanding the instructions?

Patient: No major barrier. I have transportation and someone available if symptoms change. My teach-back is: the diagnosis is acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis; I will use a clear-liquid diet briefly, advance food as pain improves, and schedule follow-up with primary care; I will use amoxicillin-clavulanate per shared decision; and I will seek help for the warning signs we reviewed.

PT: No lump or discharge. The left side still feels tighter when I reach overhead, but it has not changed.
DR: Any arm swelling or heaviness?
PT: No swelling. My sleeve fits the same.
DR: Good. On exam today I feel the expected lumpectomy scar and mild firmness from radiation, but no concerning mass and no enlarged nodes. Your right breast exam is normal.
PT: So the tight area is scar tissue?
DR: It is consistent with stable treatment-related change. If it grows or feels different, call rather than waiting for the annual visit. Your next mammogram will be due in May 2027.
PT: Okay. The bigger issue is the anastrozole. My hands and knees feel twenty years older.
DR: Tell me about the timing.
PT: It started gradually after I switched from tamoxifen about a year and a half ago. Mornings are the worst. My fingers are stiff for half an hour, and my knees complain on stairs.
DR: Does either joint become red, hot, or visibly swollen?
PT: No. Once I move around, it loosens. I can still work, but gardening takes longer. Pain is maybe five out of ten in the morning and two later.
DR: Have you missed doses because of it?
PT: Twice last month. I did not exactly forget. I wanted a day off from feeling stiff. Then I felt guilty.
DR: Thank you for saying that plainly. Side effects matter, and we should address them without judgment. An occasional missed tablet is unlikely to undo the benefit, but regular daily use gives the best protection. Before changing therapy, I would like to try a structured approach.
PT: What does that mean?
DR: Ten minutes of gentle movement before breakfast, regular walking or resistance exercise, and acetaminophen when needed. You can use up to 650 milligrams every eight hours, no more than 3,000 milligrams in a day, assuming you are not taking another acetaminophen product.
PT: I avoid ibuprofen because it bothers my stomach.
DR: That is reasonable. We do not need it. I can also refer you to physical therapy for a joint-friendly strengthening program and the shoulder tightness.
PT: I would do that. I want to keep taking the cancer medicine if we can make it manageable.
DR: That is the goal. If symptoms remain disruptive after six to eight weeks, we can discuss a short supervised break or a switch to another aromatase inhibitor. Do not stop it on your own; call us first.
PT: How much longer am I supposed to take it?
DR: You have completed about four years total of endocrine therapy, counting tamoxifen. Our current plan is at least five years. Near that point we will review your original tumor risk, tolerance, and whether extended treatment adds enough benefit for you.
PT: The bone scan worried me too. It said osteopenia. Is the medicine causing that?
DR: Aromatase inhibitors can accelerate bone loss. Your May 2024 DEXA showed mild osteopenia, not osteoporosis. You have not had a fracture, correct?
PT: Correct. No falls either.
DR: You are taking vitamin D most days?
PT: Vitamin D every morning. The calcium tablets constipate me, so I take them only a couple times a week.
DR: Let us emphasize calcium from food instead of forcing the tablets. Yogurt, fortified milk, tofu, and leafy greens can help you reach roughly 1,200 milligrams daily from food plus supplements. Continue vitamin D 1,000 units daily. Weight-bearing and resistance exercise protect bone too.
PT: When do we repeat the scan?
DR: I am ordering a DEXA for August 2026, about two years after the last one. If it has progressed, we will discuss a bone-strengthening medication and dental clearance first.
PT: My dentist is finishing a crown next month.
DR: Good to know. Finish the dental work. We are not starting a bisphosphonate today.
PT: I have also had hot flashes, mostly at night. Three or four nights a week.
DR: Are they waking you for long periods?
PT: Usually five minutes. I throw off the blanket and fall back asleep. I would rather not add another prescription.
DR: We can start with a fan, layered bedding, and limiting alcohol close to bedtime. If they become disruptive, nonhormonal medicines are available. Avoid estrogen-containing supplements unless oncology reviews them.
PT: I do drink wine with dinner, maybe four nights a week. One glass.
DR: Reducing to a few servings a week may help hot flashes and is also reasonable for breast health. Any new headaches, shortness of breath, persistent cough, abdominal pain, or focal bone pain?
PT: No. I get ordinary back soreness after gardening, but it goes away by the next day. No breathing problems.
DR: That pattern sounds mechanical, not a cancer warning symptom. We do not recommend routine CT scans or tumor-marker blood tests when someone has no concerning symptoms. Annual mammography, clinical review, and prompt evaluation of new persistent symptoms are the evidence-based surveillance plan.
PT: I wondered why nobody was scanning the rest of me. It felt like less follow-up meant less attention.
DR: I understand. More scans can find harmless abnormalities and expose you to radiation without improving outcomes for asymptomatic early-stage survivors. Less imaging does not mean less care.
PT: That explanation helps.
DR: Your recent blood count and kidney function are normal. Weight and blood pressure are stable. Mood-wise, how are you doing?
PT: Better than the first two years. Scan week still gets me. My husband calls it mammogram weather because I get quiet.
DR: Does the worry interfere with work or relationships beyond that week?
PT: Not usually. I have a survivor group online, and talking with them helps.
DR: Excellent. We can connect you with counseling if anxiety expands, but your current supports sound useful. Are you exercising now?
PT: I walk twenty minutes at lunch four days a week. I stopped the gym because my knees hurt.
DR: Keep the walking and begin resistance work gradually with physical therapy. Movement often improves aromatase-inhibitor joint symptoms despite the first few stiff minutes.
PT: That is counterintuitive, but I will try.
DR: Let us review the plan. Continue anastrozole 1 milligram daily. Continue vitamin D 1,000 units daily and aim for calcium mainly through food. I will place physical therapy and August DEXA orders. Annual mammogram is due May 2027.
PT: And acetaminophen is okay up to 3,000 milligrams?
DR: Correct, and count all products. Call for jaundice or if you develop liver disease, and do not combine it with heavy alcohol use.
PT: What should make me call the cancer clinic sooner?
DR: A new breast or underarm lump, skin or nipple change, unexplained arm swelling, persistent focal bone pain, new shortness of breath, unexplained weight loss, or neurologic symptoms. For the medication, call if joint pain prevents normal activity or makes you want to stop treatment.
PT: I appreciate you saying to call before I quit. I was close to just taking weekends off.
DR: Please do call. We have options and want the plan to be sustainable. I will see you in six months to reassess symptoms, sooner if needed.
PT: Six months works. I feel much calmer than when I walked in.
DR: I am glad. The mammogram and exam are reassuring, and you remain without clinical evidence of disease.
note:
**Subjective:** Elena Morales is a 60-year-old woman with a history of stage IA estrogen receptor-positive left upper-outer-quadrant invasive breast cancer treated with lumpectomy, radiation, and adjuvant endocrine therapy, presenting for survivorship follow-up. She completed tamoxifen initially and has taken anastrozole for approximately 18 months, about four years of total endocrine therapy. She reports morning stiffness and aching in both hands and knees, rated 5/10 on waking and improving to 2/10 with movement. There is no redness, warmth, or visible swelling. Symptoms slow stair climbing and gardening but do not prevent work. She intentionally skipped two anastrozole doses last month because of stiffness and otherwise reports adherence. She wishes to continue endocrine therapy if side effects can be controlled. She also reports brief nocturnal hot flashes three to four nights weekly but declines medication. Left breast/axillary review is negative for new mass, skin or nipple change, discharge, or arm swelling. Stable scar tightness occurs with overhead reach. No persistent focal bone pain, unexplained weight loss, cough, dyspnea, abdominal pain, or neurologic symptoms. She takes vitamin D 1,000 units daily; calcium tablets are limited by constipation. No falls or fractures. Scan-related anxiety is transient and supported by family and an online survivor group.

**Objective:** BP 126/78 mmHg; weight 71.4 kg. Well appearing. Left breast demonstrates healed lumpectomy scar and stable mild radiation fibrosis without dominant mass, skin change, or nipple abnormality. No axillary or supraclavicular adenopathy; no arm edema. Right breast exam is unremarkable. Hands and knees show no synovitis, warmth, or effusion; gait is normal. Bilateral diagnostic mammogram dated 05/28/2026 shows benign postsurgical change, BI-RADS 2, with no evidence of malignancy. Hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL and creatinine 0.78 mg/dL. Prior DEXA from 05/14/2024 demonstrated osteopenia.

**Assessment:**
1. ER-positive left breast cancer, status post breast-conserving therapy, currently without clinical or mammographic evidence of disease.
2. Aromatase inhibitor-associated arthralgia causing moderate morning symptoms and two intentionally missed doses, without inflammatory findings.
3. Osteopenia in the setting of postmenopausal status and aromatase-inhibitor exposure; no fragility fracture.
4. Mild vasomotor symptoms, currently manageable without medication.
5. Situational surveillance anxiety with intact function and effective supports.

**Plan:** Continue anastrozole 1 mg by mouth daily; medication benefit, adherence, and the importance of contacting oncology before interruption were reviewed. Begin daily gentle range-of-motion activity, continue walking, and refer to physical therapy for progressive resistance training, joint symptom management, and left shoulder/scar tightness. Acetaminophen 650 mg every 8 hours as needed may be used, maximum 3,000 mg/day from all products; she avoids NSAIDs because of dyspepsia. Reassess in 6–8 weeks by message or phone if pain remains function-limiting; options then include a supervised interruption or alternate aromatase inhibitor. Continue vitamin D3 1,000 units daily and target approximately 1,200 mg/day calcium, prioritizing food sources because supplements cause constipation. Order repeat DEXA for August 2026. No bisphosphonate is started today; complete planned dental work first and review treatment if bone loss progresses. Next annual bilateral mammogram is due May 2027. Routine systemic imaging and tumor markers are not indicated without symptoms. Reviewed return precautions for new breast/axillary mass, skin or nipple change, arm swelling, persistent focal bone pain, new dyspnea, unexplained weight loss, or neurologic symptoms. Use layered bedding/fan and reduce evening alcohol for hot flashes; avoid estrogen-containing supplements without oncology review. Follow up in survivorship clinic in six months, sooner for new symptoms or medication intolerance.

Next steps

transcript:
Triage nurse: Hello, Priya. Please tell me in your own words what brought you to urgent care today.

Patient: I cut the left forearm on a clean metal shelf while moving boxes. I was concerned it might be serious and wanted an examination. The symptoms changed enough that home care did not feel sufficient.

Triage nurse: I will document your medicines, allergies, and vital signs. Have you had fainting, severe breathing trouble, confusion, uncontrolled bleeding, or another immediate emergency symptom?

Patient: No. I have not had those problems. I can answer questions clearly, and I brought my medication list. I would like to understand what the testing means and what I should watch for at home.

Clinician: I reviewed the history, nursing assessment, medicines, allergies, and relevant prior records. On examination you are alert and appropriately interactive. Your circulation and breathing are stable. The focused examination fits the history, without a finding that requires an immediate invasive intervention.

Patient: What did the tests show? Do I need to stay in the hospital or have another procedure?

Clinician: Exploration found no tendon, nerve, vascular injury, foreign body, or contamination. Taken together with your examination, the working diagnosis is simple left forearm laceration after repair. Your response to care and current stability make discharge reasonable today. We discussed that tests reduce uncertainty but cannot predict every change after discharge.

Patient: What should I do first when I get home, and may I return to normal activity?

Clinician: Keep the dressing dry for twenty-four hours, then wash gently and return in ten days for suture removal. Start gently and increase activity only as comfort and the written restrictions allow. Do not share prescriptions, double a missed dose, or add an over-the-counter product without checking the label and possible interactions.

Patient: Please review the medicine plan. I want to make sure I heard it correctly.

Clinician: The medication plan is acetaminophen as needed. Follow the printed dose and timing. Stop and seek advice for a suspected medication reaction. Keep the follow-up appointment because improvement should be confirmed and the plan may need adjustment.

Patient: Which symptoms mean I should return right away instead of waiting for the appointment?

Clinician: Seek urgent reassessment for spreading redness, pus, fever, worsening pain, numbness, bleeding that will not stop, or reduced hand movement. Call emergency services for severe breathing difficulty, collapse, new confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms. If you are uncertain and cannot reach the clinic, emergency evaluation is appropriate.

Triage nurse: Your written instructions and follow-up information are ready. Is there any barrier to obtaining medicine, transportation, food, help at home, or understanding the instructions?

Patient: No major barrier. I have transportation and someone available if symptoms change. My teach-back is: the diagnosis is simple left forearm laceration after repair; I will keep the dressing dry for twenty-four hours, then wash gently and return in ten days for suture removal; I will use acetaminophen as needed; and I will seek help for the warning signs we reviewed.

metadata.visit_title: Psychiatry intake for recurrent panic attacks

reasonCode.text: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks

dosageInstruction.text: Take 25 mg each morning for 7 days, then 50 mg each morning if tolerated

CarePlan.title: Panic disorder treatment plan

detail.description: Weekly cognitive behavioral therapy with interoceptive exposure

transcript:
Dr. Park: Thanks for coming in, Chinedu. What made this the right time to see psychiatry?

Patient: The attacks are running my schedule. The first one happened on BART four months ago. My heart slammed, my hands tingled, and I thought I was dying. It peaked within ten minutes, but afterward I avoided the train for a week. Now they happen two or three times a week, sometimes at my desk and sometimes from sleep.

Dr. Park: Do they come only when something stressful is happening?

Patient: Not always. Work is busy, but one happened while I was watching basketball. That unpredictability is the worst part. I scan for exits and check my pulse. I drive across the bridge instead of taking transit, and I declined a concert because I pictured being trapped.

Dr. Park: During an attack, what do you notice besides the racing heart and tingling?

Patient: Short breath, sweating, pressure in my chest, and a feeling that the room is unreal. I never faint. Urgent care did an ECG and blood tests in March and said they were normal. My primary care doctor checked thyroid labs too.

Dr. Park: How is your mood between attacks?

Patient: Frustrated and embarrassed, not hopeless. I still enjoy cooking and seeing friends. My concentration slips because I am waiting for the next one. I sleep about five hours and sometimes wake with a jolt. Appetite is normal.

Dr. Park: I ask everyone directly: have you wished you were dead, thought about hurting yourself, made a plan, or attempted suicide?

Patient: No to all of that. I want my life back. I have never tried to hurt myself or anyone else.

Dr. Park: Any periods when you needed very little sleep and felt unusually energized, impulsive, or invincible? Any hallucinations or feeling watched?

Patient: No. No voices, no paranoia, and no huge bursts of energy.

Dr. Park: Alcohol, cannabis, nicotine, caffeine, or other substances?

Patient: Two beers on Saturday sometimes. No cannabis or drugs. I stopped energy drinks after the urgent-care visit. I have one coffee before nine.

Dr. Park: Tell me about medical history and medicines.

Patient: Seasonal allergies. No seizures or heart disease. I tried propranolol ten milligrams twice. It slowed my heart but made me tired, so I rarely use it. No daily medicines.

Dr. Park: Has anxiety or panic affected relatives?

Patient: My mother calls it nerves and avoids airplanes. Nobody has been hospitalized.

Dr. Park: Your symptoms fit panic disorder: repeated unexpected attacks followed by worry and avoidance. Your GAD-7 is twelve and PHQ-9 is six, but the interview does not suggest major depression, bipolar disorder, psychosis, or a substance cause. You denied suicidal and homicidal thoughts, and I do not see an acute safety concern. How does that formulation land?

Patient: Honestly, it is a relief that it has a name. I was scared you would say something was wrong with my heart despite the tests.

Dr. Park: Panic feels dangerous but is not itself a heart attack. The cycle grows when body sensations are interpreted as catastrophe and then avoided. Cognitive behavioral therapy, especially interoceptive exposure, is very effective. It deliberately and safely practices sensations like a faster heartbeat so your brain learns they pass.

Patient: I am nervous about exposure, but avoiding everything is not working.

Dr. Park: We can pace it collaboratively. I recommend weekly CBT and starting sertraline. Take twenty-five milligrams each morning for one week, then fifty milligrams if tolerated. Early nausea, loose stool, headache, sleep change, or temporary jitteriness can occur. Benefits usually build over several weeks. Rarely, mood activation or new suicidal thoughts can occur; call urgently if those appear. Do not stop suddenly after taking it regularly.

Patient: Will it change my personality or make me sedated at work?

Dr. Park: It should not change your personality. Sedation is possible but not typical; if it occurs we can move dosing to evening. I would avoid relying on benzodiazepines because they can reinforce avoidance and create dependence. You can leave propranolol unused for now.

Patient: Okay. I would like to try the therapy and medication.

Dr. Park: Before our follow-up, practice paced breathing twice daily when calm: inhale four counts and exhale six, without forcing deep breaths. Track attacks, triggers, intensity, and what you did afterward. Try one manageable step, such as riding BART one stop with a support person, after discussing the hierarchy with the therapist.

Patient: My sister would do that with me.

Dr. Park: Good. We will meet in three weeks. If you develop thoughts of self-harm, feel unable to stay safe, or have severe agitation, call 988 or go to the emergency department. For chest pain that is new, persistent, or different from the familiar attacks, seek urgent medical evaluation rather than assuming it is panic. Any final question?

Patient: No. This feels concrete. Thank you.
note:
PSYCHIATRY INTAKE

Chief concern: Recurrent unexpected panic attacks with anticipatory anxiety and avoidance.

History: Thirty-seven-year-old man reports four months of abrupt episodes featuring palpitations, dyspnea, sweating, chest pressure, paresthesias, derealization, and fear of dying. Episodes peak within approximately ten minutes and now occur two to three times weekly, including without an obvious trigger and from sleep. He has developed persistent concern, pulse checking, exit scanning, avoidance of public transit and crowded events, and occupational distraction. March urgent-care ECG and laboratory evaluation and subsequent thyroid testing were reportedly normal. Sleep is approximately five hours with occasional panic awakening; appetite and enjoyment remain intact. He denies sustained depressed mood, mania or hypomania, psychosis, trauma re-experiencing, illicit substances, and heavy alcohol use. GAD-7 12; PHQ-9 6. Propranolol 10 mg was sedating and is rarely used.

Mental status: Neatly dressed, cooperative, mildly anxious. Speech normal in rate and volume. Thought process linear and future oriented. No delusions or perceptual disturbance. Cognition grossly intact. Insight and judgment good.

Safety: Explicitly denies current or lifetime suicidal ideation, plan, intent, attempts, self-injury, and homicidal ideation. No acute intoxication, psychosis, or mania. Protective factors include treatment engagement, supportive sister, employment, friendships, and future goals. Acute risk is low; outpatient care is appropriate.

Assessment: Presentation meets criteria for panic disorder. Mild depressive symptoms appear secondary to anxiety-related impairment and do not currently meet criteria for major depressive episode. Medical and substance contributors are less likely given prior evaluation and history.

Plan: Start sertraline 25 mg by mouth each morning for seven days, then increase to 50 mg each morning if tolerated. Reviewed common gastrointestinal, headache, sleep, sexual, and transient activation effects; discussed rare mood activation and emergent suicidal thinking. Hold further propranolol use pending reassessment. Refer for weekly CBT with psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring, interoceptive exposure, and graded situational exposure. Practice paced breathing with longer exhalation twice daily and log attacks, avoidance, and recovery. Follow up in three weeks. Patient instructed to call 988 or seek emergency care for inability to remain safe, and to seek urgent medical assessment for chest symptoms that are persistent or meaningfully different from established attacks.
after_visit_summary: You were evaluated for recurrent panic attacks and avoidance; the assessment supports panic disorder. Start sertraline 25 mg each morning for 7 days, then 50 mg each morning if tolerated. Begin weekly CBT focused on panic and exposure, practice paced breathing twice daily, and track attacks. Follow up in 3 weeks. Call 988 or seek emergency care if you cannot stay safe; seek urgent evaluation for new or different persistent chest symptoms.
