CarePlan.title: Heart failure transition plan

detail.description: Daily morning weights, 2 g sodium limit, 2 L daily fluid limit, home-health visit within 48 hours, cardiology follow-up in seven days, and basic metabolic panel in three days.

transcript:
DR: Mr. Brooks, today is discharge-planning day. I asked Carla, your nurse, and your daughter Denise to join us so everyone hears the same plan. How does your breathing feel compared with Tuesday?
PT: Much better. Tuesday I could barely cross the bedroom. Today I walked past the nurses’ station without stopping. I am still tired, but I can lie flatter.
NURSE: He walked one full loop on room air this morning. Oxygen stayed at 95 percent or higher. He paused once because his legs felt weak, not because of chest pain or breathlessness.
FAMILY: His ankles look like themselves again. When I brought him in, his shoes would not close.
DR: That matches the numbers. Your admission weight was 94.8 kilograms and today it is 89.6, a loss of about 5.2 kilograms of excess fluid. You responded well to IV furosemide. Your lungs are clear enough for discharge, swelling is minimal, and kidney function is stable for you at creatinine 1.4.
PT: Did I cause this by eating salty food? I had canned soup for several days after my refrigerator broke.
DR: The sodium likely contributed, and you also missed three morning furosemide doses because you were avoiding the bathroom during a long bus trip. Heart failure exacerbations often have several triggers. This is not about blame; it tells us which safeguards can prevent another admission.
FAMILY: I did not know he had skipped pills. Dad, you have to tell me.
PT: I thought three days would not matter. I did not want to be stopping every hour.
NURSE: The water pill works for several hours, so planning the dose around travel is reasonable, but skipping without calling is risky. If a schedule problem comes up, call cardiology or the heart-failure nurse. Do not double a missed dose unless they specifically tell you to.
DR: Correct. At home, furosemide will be 40 milligrams every morning. That is a change from your old alternating 20- and 40-milligram schedule. Take potassium chloride 10 milliequivalents with it each morning until cardiology reviews your labs.
PT: Are the rest staying the same?
DR: Sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 milligrams twice daily, metoprolol succinate 50 milligrams once daily, and apixaban 5 milligrams twice daily remain the same. Continue atorvastatin as previously prescribed even though it is not one of today’s five encounter medication orders. Do not take your old furosemide instructions from the bottle you have at home. Carla will mark that bottle as replaced and the pharmacy will provide the current list.
NURSE: I have printed the grid with morning and evening columns. Denise, could you fill the weekly pill organizer with him tonight?
FAMILY: Yes. I can also take the old list off the refrigerator and put this one up.
PT: The apixaban is the blood thinner for my irregular heartbeat, right?
DR: Yes, for atrial fibrillation and stroke prevention. Do not stop it without speaking to the prescriber. Seek urgent care for uncontrolled bleeding, black stools, vomiting blood, a severe unexplained headache, or a significant fall with a head strike. Avoid ibuprofen or naproxen unless a clinician who knows you approves it because those drugs can worsen fluid retention, kidney function, and bleeding risk.
PT: I usually take ibuprofen for my knees. What can I use?
DR: Acetaminophen may be an option within label directions if you have no liver contraindication and do not combine products, but discuss ongoing knee pain with primary care. Nonmedicine approaches such as heat and gentle movement may help.
FAMILY: What exactly should he track? We have a scale, but it is in the carpeted bedroom.
NURSE: Move it to a hard, level surface. Every morning after urinating and before breakfast, wearing similar clothing, weigh yourself. Write the number on this log. Today’s discharge weight is 89.6 kilograms, or about 197.5 pounds, and that is the baseline.
PT: I use pounds. When do I call?
DR: Call the heart-failure team the same day for a gain of two pounds overnight or five pounds in one week, increasing ankle or abdominal swelling, needing more pillows, new breathlessness with ordinary activity, or reduced urination. Do not take extra furosemide on your own.
PT: And when is it an emergency?
DR: Call 911 for severe breathlessness at rest, chest pressure, fainting, blue lips, new confusion, or symptoms of stroke such as facial droop, arm weakness, or speech trouble.
FAMILY: He likes canned chili and deli turkey. We need practical food guidance, not just “low salt.”
NURSE: Aim for no more than two thousand milligrams of sodium per day. Read the sodium line on labels and look at serving size. Canned soup, chili, deli meats, frozen dinners, restaurant sauces, and salt substitutes can be problems. Rinse canned beans, choose no-salt-added versions, use herbs or lemon, and do not use a potassium-based salt substitute unless cardiology approves it because of his kidney disease and medicines.
PT: Two liters of fluid means everything I drink?
NURSE: Yes—water, coffee, tea, milk, juice, soda, soup, ice, and gelatin all count. Two liters is about 67 ounces or eight and a half eight-ounce cups. We are giving you a marked bottle to help track. Spread fluids through the day.
PT: That will take practice. My mouth gets dry.
NURSE: Small sips, sugar-free gum, ice chips counted toward the total, and mouth rinsing can help. Call if thirst becomes extreme or you feel dizzy; the plan may need adjustment, but do not change it alone.
DR: Your echocardiogram still shows an ejection fraction of 35 percent, similar to prior testing, with no new major valve problem. The admission chest film showed congestion and small effusions that improved clinically with diuresis. We are not starting an additional heart-failure medicine during this transition because of kidney function and the need for close outpatient review. Cardiology can revisit optimization.
FAMILY: What appointments are actually scheduled?
DR: Home-health nursing will visit within 48 hours to review medications, blood pressure, weight, swelling, and symptoms. A basic metabolic panel is ordered for Monday, three days after discharge, to check kidney function and potassium. Cardiology is scheduled in seven days. Primary care should see him within two weeks.
NURSE: The lab can come through home health if scheduling is confirmed today. Denise is the backup contact with Mr. Brooks’s permission.
PT: Yes, you can call Denise. She lives ten minutes away. I still want to manage my own pills.
FAMILY: I agree. I will check the organizer, not take over.
DR: That is a good plan. We also discussed pacing activity: short walks several times daily, rest before exhaustion, and no driving until you feel steady and the first outpatient review confirms the plan. Use your walker for now because deconditioning and blood-pressure medicines increase fall risk.
PT: I do get a little lightheaded when I stand fast.
NURSE: Sit at the edge of the bed first, stand slowly, and keep the walker within reach. Home health will check sitting and standing pressures. Call the same day for persistent dizziness or a systolic blood pressure below 90 if you have symptoms. Call 911 for fainting.
DR: Let’s do teach-back. Mr. Brooks, what will you do tomorrow morning?
PT: Use the scale on the kitchen floor after I urinate, write down the pounds, take 40 milligrams of furosemide with the potassium, and use the new medication sheet. I will keep sodium under two thousand milligrams and all fluids under two liters.
DR: When will you call?
PT: Two pounds overnight or five in a week, more swelling, more pillows, shortness of breath, or less urine. I will not add water pills myself. For chest pressure, severe trouble breathing, fainting, confusion, or stroke signs, Denise calls 911.
FAMILY: And I will help set up the pillbox, remove the outdated list, move the scale, and confirm Monday’s lab and next week’s cardiology visit.
NURSE: Perfect. I will send the home-health referral, provide the weight and fluid logs, and watch you take the first oral morning regimen before discharge.
DR: This is a fully synthetic training encounter rather than a real patient record. Within that scenario, the medical goals for discharge are met: stable on room air, improved volume status, stable renal function, safe mobility plan, and clear follow-up.
PT: I feel ready. I am glad Denise heard the details. I do not want to be back here next week.
DR: Neither do we. The best protection is early response to the trend, not waiting until breathing is severe. We will discharge after pharmacy reconciliation and home-health confirmation.
note:
**Subjective:** Walter Brooks is a 77-year-old synthetic patient completing discharge planning after a three-day admission for acute on chronic HFrEF exacerbation. He presented with progressive exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, bilateral edema, and rapid weight gain after several high-sodium canned meals and three missed furosemide doses during travel. He now reports substantial improvement, can lie flatter, and completed a hall loop without dyspnea or chest pain. Mild generalized fatigue and occasional positional lightheadedness persist. Patient wishes to manage his own medications; daughter Denise will support pillbox setup and monitoring.

**Objective:** Admission weight 94.8 kg; discharge weight 89.6 kg after IV loop diuresis. Morning ambulation on room air maintained oxygen saturation at or above 95%. Lungs are clear, peripheral edema is minimal, and patient is hemodynamically suitable for discharge. Creatinine is stable at 1.4 mg/dL in the setting of CKD 3a; last 24-hour urine output was 2350 mL. Admission BNP was 1260 pg/mL. Chest radiograph showed cardiomegaly, mild vascular congestion, and small bilateral effusions. Echocardiogram shows LVEF 35%, global hypokinesis, moderate left atrial enlargement, and no new significant valvular lesion.

**Assessment:**
1. Acute on chronic systolic heart failure, improved to near-euvolemia after IV diuresis; likely precipitated by excess sodium and missed diuretic doses.
2. Persistent atrial fibrillation, rate controlled, on apixaban.
3. CKD stage 3a, renal function stable through diuresis.
4. Deconditioning and mild orthostatic symptoms, with family and walker support available.

**Plan:** Discharge home today with daughter support and home-health nursing within 48 hours. Furosemide is now 40 mg orally every morning; replace the prior alternating-dose instructions and do not double missed doses or self-administer extra doses. Add potassium chloride 10 mEq each morning with furosemide until cardiology review. Continue sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate ER 50 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, and previously prescribed atorvastatin. Avoid non-prescribed NSAIDs and potassium-based salt substitutes. Use new reconciled medication list and weekly pill organizer. Obtain BMP in three days to assess creatinine and potassium. Cardiology follow-up is scheduled in seven days; primary-care follow-up within two weeks.

Measure weight each morning after voiding and before breakfast on a hard, level surface; record against discharge baseline of 89.6 kg/approximately 197.5 lb. Call the heart-failure team the same day for a two-pound overnight or five-pound weekly gain, worsening edema, increasing pillow requirement, new exertional dyspnea, reduced urine, persistent dizziness, or symptomatic systolic BP below 90. Do not adjust diuretic independently. Limit sodium to 2,000 mg/day and total fluid to 2 L/day, counting all beverages, soup, ice, and gelatin. Use walker, rise slowly, and take several short walks daily. Call 911 for severe dyspnea at rest, chest pressure, syncope, cyanosis, new confusion, or stroke symptoms. Seek urgent assessment for major bleeding, black stool, hematemesis, severe unexplained headache, or head injury while anticoagulated. Patient, nurse, and daughter completed accurate teach-back. This is a fully synthetic encounter and has not been clinically reviewed.
after_visit_summary:
Visit summary

Why you were hospitalized
• Extra fluid from heart failure caused shortness of breath, swelling, and weight gain. You improved with IV diuretic treatment.
• Discharge weight: 89.6 kg (about 197.5 lb).

Medicines
• Furosemide 40 mg every morning; stop using the old alternating-dose directions. Do not double or add doses on your own.
• Potassium chloride 10 mEq every morning with furosemide until cardiology review.
• Continue sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate ER 50 mg daily, apixaban 5 mg twice daily, and your previously prescribed atorvastatin.
• Avoid ibuprofen, naproxen, and potassium salt substitutes unless your clinician approves them.

Daily plan
• Weigh every morning after urinating and before breakfast; write it down.
• Sodium limit: 2,000 mg/day. Fluid limit: 2 L/day, including drinks, soup, ice, and gelatin.
• Use your walker, stand slowly, and take short walks.

Follow-up
• Home-health nurse within 48 hours; blood test in 3 days; cardiology in 7 days; primary care within 2 weeks.
• Call the heart-failure team for 2 lb gained overnight or 5 lb in a week, more swelling, more pillows, new shortness of breath, less urine, or persistent dizziness.
• Call 911 for severe breathing trouble at rest, chest pressure, fainting, blue lips, new confusion, or stroke signs.

This is a fully synthetic, not clinically reviewed training summary.

metadata.visit_title: CKD stage 3b and hypertension follow-up

Observation.valueString: 146/84 mmHg

dosageInstruction.text: Take one tablet daily

code.text: Renal function and urine albumin panel

DiagnosticReport.conclusion: Stable stage 3b CKD with persistent moderately increased albuminuria

CarePlan.title: Kidney protection and blood pressure plan

transcript:
MA: Mr. Okafor, your clinic pressure is 146 over 84. Did you bring your home log?
PT: Yes. I wrote morning and evening readings for two weeks.
MA: Great. Dr. Lee will review it with your laboratory results.
DR: Good morning, Chidi. How have you felt since January?
PT: Mostly normal. I would not know my kidneys were a problem if you did not check the blood.
DR: Any swelling, shortness of breath, reduced urine, blood in urine, foamy urine getting worse, nausea, itching, confusion, or unusual fatigue?
PT: No swelling or breathing trouble. Urine still looks foamy sometimes, but no blood and the amount seems normal.
DR: Any dizziness, fainting, chest pressure, severe headaches, or weakness?
PT: No.
DR: Let us look at the log. I see most mornings between 138 and 148 systolic, evenings 132 to 142, with diastolic values in the seventies and low eighties. How are you measuring?
PT: I sit at the kitchen table after breakfast, put the cuff over my shirt, and take one reading.
DR: We can make those more comparable. Avoid caffeine, exercise, and smoking for thirty minutes, empty your bladder, sit quietly five minutes with feet flat and back supported, place the cuff on bare upper arm at heart level, and take two readings one minute apart. Measure before medication and breakfast when possible.
PT: I drink coffee before almost everything, so that might be part of it.
DR: It may raise a reading temporarily, but your overall pattern and today's pressure suggest we should improve control. Are you taking losartan 100 milligrams, amlodipine 5 milligrams, and empagliflozin 10 milligrams daily?
PT: Yes. I missed two doses last month during a work trip. Otherwise every morning.
DR: Any ankle swelling from amlodipine, genital irritation, urinary infection symptoms, or lightheadedness?
PT: None. I urinate more in the morning since starting empagliflozin, but it is manageable.
DR: Your creatinine is 1.78 and estimated filtration rate 46. Last values were 1.82 and 44, so kidney filtration is stable. Potassium is 4.6 and bicarbonate 24. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 188 milligrams per gram, down from 240 but still elevated.
PT: Does stage three mean I am halfway to dialysis?
DR: No. The stage describes a range of filtration, not a countdown or percentage of kidney life. Stage 3b means eGFR between 30 and 44 in the standard classification; today's 46 is just above that boundary, but we follow the long-term trend and your established diagnosis. Many people remain stable for years, especially when blood pressure and albuminuria are treated. Nothing today suggests dialysis is near.
PT: That is a relief. What is hurting the kidneys?
DR: Long-standing high blood pressure is the leading contributor in your case. Albumin leakage is both a marker of damage and a treatment target. Losartan and empagliflozin help protect the kidneys beyond their pressure or glucose effects.
PT: My primary doctor said I do not have diabetes. Why take empagliflozin?
DR: Evidence supports this medicine for selected chronic kidney disease patients even without diabetes. We discussed benefits and risks when it was started. Hold it during significant vomiting, diarrhea, prolonged fasting, or before surgery as directed, because dehydration and rare ketoacidosis can occur. Contact us for genital infection symptoms.
PT: I take ibuprofen after basketball. Is that a problem?
DR: Yes. Regular NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen can reduce kidney blood flow and worsen pressure. Avoid them unless a clinician who knows your kidney disease specifically advises otherwise. Acetaminophen within labeled dosing is generally preferred for occasional pain, but review persistent pain with us.
PT: What change are we making for pressure?
DR: Increase amlodipine from 5 to 10 milligrams daily. Continue losartan 100 and empagliflozin 10. Watch for ankle swelling, flushing, or dizziness. Send a properly measured seven-day log in two weeks. Our usual target is under 130 over 80 when tolerated, based on standardized readings and your albuminuria.
PT: Could the higher dose damage the kidneys?
DR: Amlodipine does not directly injure the kidneys. Better pressure control is protective. We will assess symptoms and readings rather than chase a low number.
DR: Maintain hydration during heat and exercise. If you have vomiting or diarrhea and cannot drink, call for sick-day medication guidance rather than guessing. Do not start herbal cleanses or supplements without checking; some contain undeclared substances.
PT: How often do we check labs?
DR: Repeat kidney panel, potassium, and urine albumin in about three months. Because today's values are stable and we are changing amlodipine rather than losartan, an immediate potassium check is not required. Call sooner for marked swelling, faintness, very low readings, reduced urine, blood in urine, or new shortness of breath.
DR: Please summarize what you will do.
PT: Increase amlodipine to ten, keep losartan and empagliflozin, avoid ibuprofen and salt substitutes, measure before coffee with two readings, and send a seven-day log in two weeks. Labs and follow-up in three months.
DR: Perfect. The dietitian will call you about sodium and moderate protein.
note:
**Subjective:** Chidi Okafor is a 51-year-old man with CKD stage 3b, hypertension, and persistent albuminuria. He feels well and denies edema, dyspnea, oliguria, gross hematuria, nausea, pruritus, confusion, chest pain, syncope, severe headache, or focal weakness. Intermittent foamy urine is unchanged. Two-week home log shows systolic readings mostly 138-148 mornings and 132-142 evenings. He measures after coffee, over clothing, without a rest period. He reports good adherence to losartan 100 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, and empagliflozin 10 mg aside from two travel-related omissions. No edema, dizziness, genital symptoms, or urinary infection. He uses ibuprofen after basketball and recently added protein shakes.

**Objective:** Clinic BP 146/84 mmHg. Creatinine 1.78 mg/dL, eGFR 46 mL/min/1.73 m2, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, and urine albumin/creatinine ratio 188 mg/g. Prior creatinine 1.82, eGFR 44, and UACR 240. Kidney function is stable with improved but persistent albuminuria.

**Assessment:** Proteinuric CKD, historically stage 3b, stable without electrolyte, acid-base, volume, or uremic complication. Hypertension remains above target based on clinic and home pattern, though home technique needs standardization. Persistent albuminuria is treated with maximal losartan and an SGLT2 inhibitor.

**Plan:** Increase amlodipine to 10 mg daily; monitor for edema, flushing, dizziness, and symptomatic hypotension. Continue losartan 100 mg and empagliflozin 10 mg daily. Reviewed SGLT2 sick-day holding during significant vomiting, diarrhea, prolonged fasting, or perioperative periods and advised calling for guidance. Measure BP before caffeine/medications after five minutes seated, cuff on bare arm, two readings one minute apart. Submit a seven-day log in two weeks; target generally below 130/80 if tolerated. Avoid NSAIDs and unreviewed supplements; acetaminophen within label directions is preferred for occasional pain. Avoid potassium salt substitutes and high-protein supplements; no blanket fruit restriction with current potassium. Aim for sodium below 2 g/day and moderate protein intake; renal dietitian referral placed. Repeat renal panel, potassium, and UACR in three months. Seek urgent care for chest pain, severe dyspnea, confusion, syncope, focal weakness, or severe symptomatic hypertension. Call sooner for reduced urine, hematuria, marked edema, or persistent low readings.
after_visit_summary: Increase amlodipine to 10 mg daily; continue losartan and empagliflozin. Check pressure before coffee after resting, take two readings, and send a seven-day log in two weeks. Avoid ibuprofen/naproxen, salt substitutes, high-protein supplements, and unreviewed herbs. Repeat kidney labs in three months.

metadata.visit_title: Upper-GI-bleed hospital discharge

condition_labels: stabilized upper gastrointestinal bleed from gastric ulcer

reasonCode.text: was hospitalized for black stools and dizziness from a bleeding gastric ulcer

code.text: stabilized upper gastrointestinal bleed from gastric ulcer

Observation.valueString: endoscopy treated the ulcer, hemoglobin remained stable afterward, and she tolerated meals without recurrent bleeding

transcript:
Triage nurse: Hello, Helen. Please tell me in your own words what brought you to inpatient discharge today.

Patient: I was hospitalized for black stools and dizziness from a bleeding gastric ulcer. I was concerned it might be serious and wanted an examination. The symptoms changed enough that home care did not feel sufficient.

Triage nurse: I will document your medicines, allergies, and vital signs. Have you had fainting, severe breathing trouble, confusion, uncontrolled bleeding, or another immediate emergency symptom?

Patient: No. I have not had those problems. I can answer questions clearly, and I brought my medication list. I would like to understand what the testing means and what I should watch for at home.

Clinician: I reviewed the history, nursing assessment, medicines, allergies, and relevant prior records. On examination you are alert and appropriately interactive. Your circulation and breathing are stable. The focused examination fits the history, without a finding that requires an immediate invasive intervention.

Patient: What did the tests show? Do I need to stay in the hospital or have another procedure?

Clinician: Endoscopy treated the ulcer, hemoglobin remained stable afterward, and she tolerated meals without recurrent bleeding. Taken together with your examination, the working diagnosis is stabilized upper gastrointestinal bleed from gastric ulcer. Your response to care and current stability make discharge reasonable today. We discussed that tests reduce uncertainty but cannot predict every change after discharge.

Patient: What should I do first when I get home, and may I return to normal activity?

Clinician: Take pantoprazole exactly as prescribed, avoid nsaids and alcohol, and attend gastroenterology follow-up. Start gently and increase activity only as comfort and the written restrictions allow. Do not share prescriptions, double a missed dose, or add an over-the-counter product without checking the label and possible interactions.

Patient: Please review the medicine plan. I want to make sure I heard it correctly.

Clinician: The medication plan is pantoprazole twice daily. Follow the printed dose and timing. Stop and seek advice for a suspected medication reaction. Keep the follow-up appointment because improvement should be confirmed and the plan may need adjustment.

Patient: Which symptoms mean I should return right away instead of waiting for the appointment?

Clinician: Seek urgent reassessment for vomiting blood, recurrent black stools, fainting, chest pain, severe weakness, or shortness of breath. Call emergency services for severe breathing difficulty, collapse, new confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms. If you are uncertain and cannot reach the clinic, emergency evaluation is appropriate.

Triage nurse: Your written instructions and follow-up information are ready. Is there any barrier to obtaining medicine, transportation, food, help at home, or understanding the instructions?

Patient: No major barrier. I have transportation and someone available if symptoms change. My teach-back is: the diagnosis is stabilized upper gastrointestinal bleed from gastric ulcer; I will take pantoprazole exactly as prescribed, avoid NSAIDs and alcohol, and attend gastroenterology follow-up; I will use pantoprazole twice daily; and I will seek help for the warning signs we reviewed.

Clinician: That summary is accurate. Questions were answered, and you are leaving in stable condition with a clear follow-up and return plan.
note:

Helen Morris is a patient seen in inpatient discharge after they was hospitalized for black stools and dizziness from a bleeding gastric ulcer. History was obtained directly from the patient or accompanying caregiver and reconciled with the available medication and allergy list. The patient sought evaluation because symptoms persisted or changed despite reasonable home measures. They deny syncope, confusion, severe respiratory distress, or uncontrolled bleeding unless otherwise described above. Access to transportation, medication, and home observation was confirmed.

Focused examination: Alert, appropriately interactive, and in no acute distress at disposition. Breathing is unlabored and circulation is clinically stable. The targeted examination is consistent with the presenting history and reveals no immediate procedural or resuscitation indication. Relevant diagnostic review: endoscopy treated the ulcer, hemoglobin remained stable afterward, and she tolerated meals without recurrent bleeding. The results and their limitations were explained in plain language, with time for questions.

Assessment: Stabilized upper gastrointestinal bleed from gastric ulcer. Current findings, clinical course, and response to treatment support the documented level of care and discharge plan. No present feature requires escalation, though evolving illness or injury remains possible and was addressed through explicit precautions.

Plan: Take pantoprazole exactly as prescribed, avoid nsaids and alcohol, and attend gastroenterology follow-up. Medication plan: pantoprazole twice daily. The patient will follow printed dosing, avoid sharing or doubling medication, and check labels before combining nonprescription products. Follow-up should occur as stated in the discharge paperwork so recovery, function, and treatment tolerance can be reassessed.

Return urgently for vomiting blood, recurrent black stools, fainting, chest pain, severe weakness, or shortness of breath. Call emergency services for collapse, severe breathing difficulty, new confusion, or rapidly worsening symptoms. Patient or caregiver completed teach-back of diagnosis, treatment, follow-up, and warning signs. Questions were answered, practical barriers were assessed, and the patient was stable at disposition.

Medication plan: pantoprazole twice daily. Seek urgent care for vomiting blood, recurrent black stools, fainting, chest pain, severe weakness, or shortness of breath. Follow the written follow-up plan.

metadata.visit_title: Week-ten ACL reconstruction rehabilitation follow-up

condition_labels: Rupture of anterior cruciate ligament of right knee

reasonCode.text: Rehabilitation after right ACL reconstruction

code.text: Right knee active range of motion

CarePlan.title: ACL rehabilitation phase-three plan

detail.description: Progress closed-chain strength, single-leg control, and low-impact conditioning without cutting or running

transcript:
Therapist: Welcome back, Elena. You are ten weeks out from the right ACL reconstruction. Give me the honest version of this week, not the highlight reel.

Patient: The knee feels mostly normal walking around campus. I get a dull ache after stairs, maybe a two out of ten. Swelling is less, but it puffs slightly after I stand through my lab. I have not had giving way or locking.

Therapist: Any sharp pain, calf pain, numbness, fever, or trouble with the incisions?

Patient: No. The scars are closed. No calf pain or numbness.

Therapist: How often did the home program happen?

Patient: Four days. I was supposed to do five, but I had exams. I did the bike, bridges, squats, step-downs, and band walks. I skipped one day because the knee was sore after I tried jogging across a street.

Therapist: Jogging was not in the plan yet. What happened?

Patient: The light changed and I panicked. It was maybe six steps. Nothing popped, but it felt awkward and I worried afterward.

Therapist: I appreciate you telling me. Your graft is still biologically remodeling even when daily life feels easy. A brief accidental jog without swelling, instability, or loss of motion is reassuring, but planned running waits for strength and control criteria. Let us check the response. Walk to the end and back.

Patient: It feels smooth.

Therapist: Gait is symmetrical. I see trace joint fullness, no warmth. Extension reaches zero degrees and flexion is one hundred thirty-two. That is excellent motion. Hold the quad set. Good. Now relax. Your right quadriceps is still visibly smaller. On dynamometer testing today, peak force is sixty-eight percent of the left side.

Patient: That sounds low. I thought I was stronger.

Therapist: It is common at ten weeks and exactly why we measure. Walking can hide a large deficit. For running, I want at least eighty percent symmetry plus good single-leg mechanics, surgeon clearance, and no reactive swelling. Return to cutting sport requires a later, more demanding battery, usually at nine months or beyond, not just a calendar date.

Patient: Soccer tryouts are in October. Am I already behind?

Therapist: You are not behind. Your motion and symptoms are on track; quadriceps capacity is the current limiter. We can improve it with consistent loading. Let us see your step-down from the six-inch box.

Patient: Like this?

Therapist: Slow for three seconds. Keep the kneecap over the second toe. Your pelvis drops and the knee moves inward on the last few reps. Use the rail lightly and reduce the depth. Better. What do you feel?

Patient: Thigh burning, no knee pain.

Therapist: Perfect target. Now split squats, right leg forward. Keep your trunk slightly forward. Eight repetitions.

Patient: The last two shake a lot.

Therapist: Shaking is fatigue, not damage, as long as alignment and pain stay controlled. We will do three sets of eight. Next is single-leg press at a load you can move cleanly, then hamstring bridges and lateral band walks.

Patient: Can I use the elliptical? The bike is boring.

Therapist: Yes, start ten minutes at easy resistance. If pain stays at three or less and swelling is not worse that evening or the next morning, add two to three minutes every few sessions, up to twenty. No running, jumping, pivoting, or open-field soccer drills yet.

Patient: What about passing a ball while standing?

Therapist: Stationary short passing with both feet planted is reasonable if the surface is level and nobody challenges you. No reaching, twisting, or reactive drills. Wear supportive shoes.

Patient: Got it. How do I judge swelling?

Therapist: Compare the kneecap outline and how easily the knee bends each morning. A small temporary ache is acceptable. If swelling or pain rises and stays elevated into the next day, reduce the previous session by about twenty-five percent and use compression and elevation. Call the surgeon for a new pop with rapid swelling, true giving way, locked motion, marked calf swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

Patient: I have been icing automatically every night. Is that necessary?

Therapist: Ice is optional for comfort now; it does not replace load management. Ten to fifteen minutes with cloth protecting the skin is fine if it helps.

Patient: Can we make the schedule realistic around classes?

Therapist: Absolutely. Strength Monday, Wednesday, and Saturday; brief mobility and balance Tuesday and Friday; easy bike or elliptical two or three days. One full rest day. I am updating the program with split squats, controlled step-downs, single-leg press, bridges, band walks, and single-leg balance with reaches.

Patient: Three strength days feels doable.

Therapist: Great. Today pain remained two out of ten, motion stayed full, and mechanics improved with cues. We will repeat strength testing in four weeks and see you twice weekly until then. Bring questions rather than experimenting with running.

Patient: Deal. I want to earn it, not set myself back.
note:
PHYSICAL THERAPY PROGRESS NOTE

Diagnosis: Right ACL rupture, status post reconstruction ten weeks ago.

Subjective: Twenty-three-year-old college student reports minimal pain with routine walking and intermittent 2/10 anterior ache and mild swelling after prolonged standing or stairs. She completed the home program four days this week. She briefly jogged approximately six steps to cross a street; there was no pop, instability, rapid swelling, or subsequent loss of motion. Denies locking, giving way, sharp pain, calf pain, fever, numbness, or incision concern. Goal remains return to recreational soccer, with anticipated tryouts in October.

Objective: Gait symmetrical without assistive device. Incisions closed; trace effusion without warmth. Right knee active range of motion 0 degrees extension to 132 degrees flexion. Quadriceps dynamometry limb symmetry index 68%. Six-inch step-down demonstrates ipsilateral pelvic drop and dynamic knee valgus with fatigue, improved using reduced depth, light rail support, and verbal cueing. Patient completed split squats, controlled step-downs, single-leg press, hamstring bridges, lateral band walks, and balance reaches. Post-exercise pain 2/10 without increased effusion.

Assessment: Motion and symptom control are appropriate for postoperative week ten. Persistent right quadriceps weakness and impaired frontal-plane control limit readiness for running, jumping, pivoting, and sport. No reported or observed findings suggest acute graft complication after the brief accidental jog. Patient benefits from measurable criteria and demonstrated improved movement quality with cues.

Plan: Continue physical therapy twice weekly. Home strength program Monday, Wednesday, and Saturday: split squats, three-second step-downs, single-leg press, hamstring bridges, and lateral band walks. Mobility and single-leg balance Tuesday and Friday. Begin easy elliptical for 10 minutes; increase by 2 to 3 minutes every several sessions to a maximum of 20 minutes if pain remains 3/10 or less and no swelling persists the next morning. No running, jumping, cutting, pivoting, or reactive soccer drills. Stationary short passing is permitted on a level surface without reaching or twisting. Reassess quadriceps strength in four weeks; running requires at least 80% limb symmetry, acceptable single-leg mechanics, no reactive effusion, and surgeon clearance. Reduce load approximately 25% after a next-day symptom increase. Seek surgical or urgent assessment for new pop with rapid swelling, true instability, locked motion, marked calf swelling, chest pain, or dyspnea.
after_visit_summary: Your knee motion is 0 to 132 degrees and walking is symmetrical. Right quadriceps strength is 68% of the left, so continue progressive strength and control work; do not run, jump, cut, pivot, or perform reactive soccer drills yet. Start easy elliptical at 10 minutes and progress only without next-day swelling. Attend PT twice weekly and repeat strength testing in 4 weeks. Seek care for a new pop with rapid swelling, true giving way, locking, marked calf swelling, chest pain, or shortness of breath.

metadata.visit_title: Neurology consultation — chronic migraine and medication-overuse headache

reasonCode.text: Increasing migraine frequency

code.text: Acute headache medication days per month

dosageInstruction.text: Take 25 mg nightly for 7 days, then 25 mg twice daily; contact clinic before further titration
Take 50 mg at migraine onset; may repeat once after 2 hours; maximum 100 mg/day and no more than 2 days/week

CarePlan.title: Chronic migraine and medication-overuse reduction plan

detail.description: Headache diary, preventive titration, and acute-medication limit

transcript:
DR: Ms. Patel, I am Dr. Varga. I read the referral, but I want the headache story in your words, starting with the earliest headaches you remember.
PT: I had occasional migraines in college—one every few months. Over the last year they became weekly, and since January my head hurts more days than it does not.
DR: How many days in a typical month have any headache?
PT: I tracked April after my primary doctor asked. Eighteen days. Nine were the really bad kind.
DR: Describe a bad one.
PT: Usually throbbing behind my right eye, sometimes both temples. Light and ordinary sounds feel sharp. I get nauseated but rarely vomit. If I move around, it pounds harder. I want a dark room.
DR: Any visual zigzags, blind spots, tingling, trouble speaking, or weakness before pain?
PT: No. My vision gets hard to focus once pain is strong, but no warning aura.
DR: How long untreated?
PT: Half a day, sometimes into the next morning. Sumatriptan can stop it in two hours if I take it early.
DR: What about the other nine headache days?
PT: Dull pressure across my forehead, three or four out of ten. I can work through those with ibuprofen.
DR: Let us count all acute medication days, not pills. In April, how many days did you use ibuprofen?
PT: Maybe fourteen. I keep a bottle at my desk and take 600 milligrams. Some days I repeat it.
DR: Sumatriptan days?
PT: Six or seven. Sometimes on a day I already took ibuprofen.
DR: So acute treatment on roughly seventeen distinct days. That frequency can itself maintain headaches, a pattern called medication-overuse headache.
PT: I was afraid you would say the medicine caused everything. I need it to work.
DR: You did not cause this, and the medicines are not bad. A migraine-prone brain exposed to frequent rescue treatment can become more sensitive. We need a preventive plan while reducing rescue days so you are not simply left in pain.
PT: Is this something dangerous, like a tumor?
DR: We will screen carefully. Did these headaches reach maximum intensity like a thunderclap within one minute?
PT: Never. They build over thirty minutes.
DR: New headache with fever, stiff neck, cancer, immune suppression, pregnancy, head injury, coughing, exertion, or position? Does it wake you from sleep?
PT: No fever or injury. I am not pregnant. Bending over makes a migraine pound if it is already there, but does not start one. It does not wake me from sleep.
DR: Any progressive vision loss, double vision, weakness, numbness, imbalance, fainting, seizure, or personality change?
PT: No.
DR: Family history?
PT: My mother and older sister both have migraines.
DR: Your pattern, family history, and normal examination are reassuring for migraine without aura. There are no current red flags requiring urgent imaging. We reconsider imaging if the pattern changes or examination becomes abnormal.
PT: That is a relief. Why did it get so frequent?
DR: Often several factors. Tell me about sleep, caffeine, meals, hydration, and stress.
PT: I manage a software support team. We cover early East Coast tickets, so I wake at five thirty. I sleep around six hours and catch up on weekends. Three large coffees most workdays. Breakfast is optional. I drink water when I remember.
DR: Anxiety?
PT: Better on sertraline 50, but work has been relentless. No panic attacks lately.
DR: Any depression or self-harm thoughts?
PT: No. I am frustrated, not depressed.
DR: What preventive migraine medicines have you tried?
PT: Propranolol two years ago. It made me lightheaded during yoga, and my pulse was in the fifties. Amitriptyline made me groggy and hungry. Neither lasted two months.
DR: Other health concerns—kidney stones, glaucoma, asthma, low blood pressure, liver disease?
PT: No stones or glaucoma. Blood pressure tends to be normal-low.
DR: Pregnancy plans or contraception matter for preventive choice.
PT: I have a hormonal IUD and do not plan pregnancy in the next few years.
DR: Topiramate is one option. It can cause tingling, slowed word-finding or thinking, appetite change, and rarely kidney stones or acute eye pain. It can harm a fetus, and at higher doses can affect hormonal contraception. Your IUD is highly effective, but contact us before any pregnancy attempt and stop to seek urgent care for sudden eye pain or vision change.
PT: My job depends on words. The cognitive side effect worries me.
DR: Reasonable. We start low: 25 milligrams nightly for one week, then 25 twice daily. Do not increase further until you tell us how cognition and tingling are. Alternatives include a CGRP-targeting medication, though insurance often requires trials first. You are part of the decision; if word-finding becomes meaningful, contact us and we stop or change course.
PT: I can try low and slow.
DR: For the medication-overuse piece, I recommend stopping daily ibuprofen rather than tapering it. Headaches may temporarily worsen for several days, sometimes up to two weeks. Limit all acute headache medication combined to no more than two days per week.
PT: What do I do on the other days if it is bad?
DR: Non-drug measures—hydration, regular meal, dark quiet room, cool pack, relaxation breathing. This is the hard part, which is why we start prevention now and arrange a nurse call in two weeks. If withdrawal is unmanageable, call; do not silently return to daily dosing.
PT: Can I keep sumatriptan?
DR: Yes. Use 50 milligrams at the first clear migraine symptom, may repeat once after two hours, maximum 100 milligrams in a day. Count it toward the two-days-per-week total. Do not combine with another triptan. Your current sertraline and sumatriptan are commonly used together; serotonin toxicity is rare, but seek care for severe agitation, fever, marked tremor, or rigid muscles.
PT: I did not know medication days mattered more than pill count.
DR: Keep a diary with headache day, migraine features, medication, menstrual timing, sleep, and functional impact. The goal is at least a 50 percent reduction in monthly migraine days after an adequate preventive trial, not instant zero.
PT: What changes actually help besides perfect sleep, which is not realistic?
DR: Consistency matters more than perfection. Move caffeine toward two servings daily, at similar times, without abrupt withdrawal. Eat something with protein within an hour of waking. Carry water and aim for pale-yellow urine. Keep wake time within about one hour even on weekends. Moderate aerobic exercise three times weekly, building gradually.

PT: Okay.

DR: Correct, based on this stable phenotype and normal exam. Seek urgent evaluation for a sudden worst headache peaking within a minute, headache with fever and stiff neck, new weakness, confusion, seizure, fainting, or persistent vision loss. Contact us promptly for a major pattern change.

DR: We judge after reaching a tolerated dose and giving it about eight to twelve weeks. Nurse call in two weeks, clinic follow-up in eight weeks. Bring the diary.
PT: And no ibuprofen starting tomorrow?
DR: Stop the frequent ibuprofen now. Sumatriptan remains available within the combined two-day weekly limit. Avoid replacing ibuprofen with acetaminophen or a caffeine combination every day, because that perpetuates the cycle.
PT: Understood. It sounds unpleasant but finite.
DR: Exactly. The expected rough patch is temporary, and you have a contact plan.
note:
**Subjective:** Nisha Patel is a 33-year-old woman referred for increasing headache frequency. She reports 18 headache days in April, 9 with migrainous features: gradual-onset throbbing retro-orbital/temporal pain, photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, movement sensitivity, and duration up to the next morning. She has no aura. Other days are milder bifrontal pressure. She used ibuprofen 600 mg on approximately 14 days and sumatriptan on 6-7 days, totaling about 17 acute-treatment days. Sumatriptan is effective when taken early. No thunderclap onset, fever, positional or exertional initiation, nocturnal awakening, progressive visual loss, focal deficit, seizure, trauma, cancer, immunosuppression, or pregnancy. Family history is positive for migraine. Sleep is irregular at about six hours, she often skips breakfast, uses three large coffees daily, and has inconsistent hydration. Anxiety is improved on sertraline 50 mg; no depression or suicidality. Propranolol caused symptomatic bradycardia and amitriptyline caused sedation/weight gain. She has a hormonal IUD and no near-term pregnancy plans.

**Objective:** BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 76/min. Well appearing. Funduscopic examination shows sharp discs. Mental status, cranial nerves, strength, sensation, reflexes, coordination, and gait including tandem are normal.

**Assessment:**
1. Chronic migraine without aura: 18 headache days/month with at least 9 migraine-feature days, strong family history, and normal neurologic examination. No current red flags requiring neuroimaging.
2. Medication-overuse headache from acute therapy on approximately 17 days/month.
3. Generalized anxiety, stable on sertraline.

**Plan:**
- Start topiramate 25 mg nightly for 7 days, then 25 mg twice daily. Do not titrate further until tolerability review. Discussed paresthesia, cognitive/word-finding effects, appetite change, kidney stones, rare acute eye pain, teratogenicity, and contraception considerations. Contact clinic for meaningful cognitive symptoms; urgent care for sudden eye pain/vision change. Contact neurology before pregnancy planning.
- Stop frequent ibuprofen. Temporary worsening for days to two weeks was discussed. Limit all acute headache medications combined to no more than 2 days/week; do not substitute daily acetaminophen or caffeine combinations.
- Continue sumatriptan 50 mg at migraine onset, repeat once after 2 hours if needed, maximum 100 mg/day and within the 2-days/week combined limit. Serotonin-toxicity warning signs reviewed with concurrent sertraline.
- Maintain diary of headache days, migraine features, acute medication, menstrual timing, sleep, and function.
- Regular protein-containing breakfast, consistent hydration, stable wake time, gradual reduction to two caffeine servings, and moderate aerobic exercise three times weekly.
- No imaging now; reassess if phenotype or examination changes. Emergency precautions: thunderclap headache, fever/stiff neck, new weakness, confusion, seizure, fainting, or persistent vision loss.
- Nurse call in 2 weeks; neurology follow-up in 8 weeks with diary. Evaluate preventive efficacy after 8-12 weeks at a tolerated dose.

• Medication-overuse headache
• Preventive treatment and rescue-medication limits

metadata.visit_title: Rheumatoid arthritis flare — disease control and DMARD safety monitoring

dosageInstruction.text: Take 8 tablets (20 mg total) by mouth once weekly on Sunday
Take 1 tablet by mouth daily except on methotrexate day
Take 15 mg daily for 3 days, then 10 mg daily for 3 days, then 5 mg daily for 3 days, then stop

DiagnosticReport.conclusion: CBC, creatinine, and transaminases are within monitoring parameters. CRP is elevated at 14.8 mg/L.

transcript:
DR: Hi, Nikhil. I saw your portal message about swollen hands. How are they today?
PT: Better than Saturday, but still bad. I could not close my right hand when I woke up.
DR: When did this change start?
PT: About three weeks ago. First the knuckles felt tender, then both wrists and my left foot joined in. Morning stiffness is close to two hours now.
DR: Before this, how long did stiffness usually last?
PT: Fifteen or twenty minutes. I had been doing well for months.
DR: Any trigger you can identify, such as an infection, missed medicine, major stress, or travel?
PT: I had a cold in March, no fever. Work has been chaotic. I also missed two Sunday methotrexate doses.
DR: Tell me what happened with the doses.
PT: The pharmacy said the prescription was too early, then I traveled for my sister's wedding. I forgot to move the pills into my bag. I restarted last Sunday.
DR: You normally take eight 2.5-milligram tablets together, for 20 milligrams once weekly?
PT: Yes, all eight after dinner on Sunday. Never daily.
DR: Good. I always verify because daily methotrexate dosing can be dangerous. You also take folic acid?
PT: One milligram every day except Sunday. Hydroxychloroquine twice a day too.
DR: Any nausea, mouth sores, unusual bruising, shortness of breath, or hair loss?
PT: Mild nausea Monday morning, but no sores or bruising. Breathing is normal.
DR: Fever, chills, productive cough, painful urination, or open skin infection now?
PT: None. The cold is completely gone.
DR: Let us map the joints. You mentioned knuckles, wrists, and left forefoot. What about elbows, shoulders, knees, or ankles?
PT: Right elbow aches but is not swollen. Knees are okay. The left ankle feels stiff, and the balls of that foot hurt when I first stand.
DR: On exam I count swelling in six knuckle joints and both wrists, and tenderness in several more hand joints plus the left second and third toe joints. This does look like an inflammatory rheumatoid flare, not only overuse.
PT: I was afraid the methotrexate stopped working.
DR: Missing two weeks can allow disease activity to return, and methotrexate takes time to regain its effect. Your CRP is elevated at 14.8, which supports active inflammation. The reassuring part is that your blood counts, liver enzymes, and kidney function are within safe monitoring ranges.
PT: Do I need a stronger medicine now?
DR: Maybe, but I do not want to decide from a flare immediately after interrupted therapy. We will continue methotrexate 20 milligrams weekly and hydroxychloroquine 200 milligrams twice daily, treat this flare briefly, and reassess in about six weeks.
PT: What will treat it quickly? I type all day, and this week has been rough.
DR: A nine-day prednisone taper: 15 milligrams daily for three days, then 10 daily for three days, then 5 daily for three days, then stop. Take it in the morning with food.
PT: Steroids make me hungry and irritable.
DR: That can happen. The course is deliberately short. It can also raise blood pressure, glucose, and infection risk. Call for fever or concerning infection symptoms. If mood changes become severe, stop and call.
PT: Could I use ibuprofen instead?
DR: You have reflux and previously had stomach pain on naproxen. A short steroid taper is likely safer and more effective for this degree of synovitis. Acetaminophen can help pain but does not control the inflammation.
PT: Okay. What happens if I am still swollen after six weeks?
DR: Then we discuss escalation. Options include injectable methotrexate for better absorption or adding a biologic medicine. Before a biologic, we would update tuberculosis and hepatitis screening and review vaccines.
PT: I would rather not do injections, but I also do not want damaged joints.
DR: That tradeoff deserves a shared decision, not a rushed choice today. Persistent inflammation can damage joints, so our target is low disease activity or remission. I want you to send a message in two weeks about morning stiffness and swelling, then return in six weeks.
PT: Should I continue methotrexate during the prednisone?
DR: Yes. Continue the Sunday dose. Hold methotrexate and call us if you develop a significant infection, fever, need antibiotics, or have surgery instructions. Do not take trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole unless the prescriber coordinates with us because it can interact dangerously.
PT: That is the antibiotic called Bactrim, right?
DR: Correct. Also avoid excess alcohol. How much are you drinking?
PT: One beer Friday and maybe one Saturday. Never on methotrexate day.
DR: That limited amount is unlikely to be a problem with normal liver tests, but keep it modest and avoid alcohol if liver enzymes rise.
PT: The lab report had several numbers flagged in the portal. Was my liver okay?
DR: AST is 26 and ALT 31, both acceptable. Hemoglobin is 14.2, white count 6.1, platelets 248, and creatinine 0.94. No cytopenia, liver injury, or kidney impairment. The inflammatory marker, CRP, is the meaningful high result today.
PT: How often do I need those tests?
DR: CBC, liver enzymes, and creatinine every eight weeks for now, especially while disease control is unsettled. If stable later, we may space them to every twelve weeks. Next labs are due the week of June 8.
PT: I can do them at the lab near my office.
DR: Good. We will send standing orders. When was your last eye examination for hydroxychloroquine?
PT: Last July. They dilated my eyes and did a field test.
DR: Excellent. Annual retinal screening is due again by July 2026. Any visual blind spots, color change, or trouble reading?
PT: No changes.
DR: Vaccines matter with immune-modifying medicines. You had influenza last fall and the updated COVID vaccine, correct?
PT: Yes. I got the shingles series two years ago.
DR: Good. Avoid live vaccines while immunosuppressed. Routine non-live vaccines are appropriate.
PT: Is it okay to exercise during a flare?
DR: Gentle range of motion and low-impact activity are useful. Avoid forceful gripping or high-impact exercise across a hot, swollen joint. Occupational therapy can suggest hand splints and ways to protect joints while typing.
PT: A splint might help. My wrist bends when I sleep.
DR: I will refer you to occupational therapy. They can fit a neutral wrist support and assess your workstation. Heat in the morning may ease stiffness; cold packs after activity may reduce swelling.
PT: My wife keeps telling me to stop working through pain. She is probably right.
DR: Pacing helps. Short movement breaks every thirty to forty-five minutes are better than holding one posture for hours. Do you need a temporary work note?
PT: Maybe for voice dictation and extra breaks, not time off.
DR: I can write that accommodation for six weeks.
PT: Thank you. Another question: can I take turmeric? My cousin says it cured his inflammation.
DR: Evidence for supplements is inconsistent, and products vary. Turmeric can upset the stomach and interact with medicines affecting bleeding. I would not substitute it for a DMARD. Bring any product label before starting it.
PT: Fair enough.
DR: Your blood pressure is 138 over 84, a little above your usual but not urgent. Prednisone may increase it. Check at home twice weekly during the taper and contact primary care if readings repeatedly exceed 160 over 100.
PT: I have a cuff. I take losartan every morning.
DR: Continue that. Let us make sure the prescription issue does not recur. Would a ninety-day methotrexate supply and pharmacy reminder help?
PT: Yes. The app reminder would help before travel too.
DR: I will renew ninety days with appropriate monitoring and ask the pharmacist to synchronize refills. Methotrexate stays once weekly on Sunday. Folic acid stays daily except Sunday.
PT: And the hydroxychloroquine stays the same?
DR: Yes, 200 milligrams twice daily. We did not generate a new order today because your supply is current.
PT: What symptoms mean I should not wait six weeks?
DR: Fever, breathing difficulty, rapidly worsening weakness, a red extremely painful single joint, medication rash, mouth sores that prevent eating, unusual bleeding, or severe prednisone mood symptoms. Contact us if swelling does not begin improving within a week.
PT: I will. This feels more manageable now.
DR: Good. Start prednisone tomorrow morning, continue your DMARDs, complete labs the week of June 8, send an update in two weeks, and return in six weeks.
PT: I wrote it down. Thank you for going through the lab numbers instead of just saying they were fine.
DR: You are welcome. Understanding the monitoring is part of safely using these medicines.
note:
**Subjective:** Nikhil Patel is a 49-year-old man with RF/CCP-positive rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate 20 mg weekly, folic acid, and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily, presenting with three weeks of increased inflammatory joint symptoms. He reports approximately two hours of morning stiffness, inability to fully close the right hand on waking, and pain/swelling in bilateral MCP joints, wrists, left ankle, and left forefoot. Baseline morning stiffness was 15–20 minutes with good function. He missed two consecutive weekly methotrexate doses because of a refill problem and travel, then resumed the correct once-weekly dose last Sunday. He denies current fever, chills, respiratory or urinary infection symptoms. Mild post-dose nausea is unchanged; no oral ulcers, unusual bruising, dyspnea, or alopecia. He has GERD and prior abdominal pain with naproxen. Work requires prolonged typing, which is impaired by hand and wrist symptoms. Last hydroxychloroquine retinal screening was July 2025; no visual symptoms. Influenza, COVID, and recombinant zoster immunizations are current. Alcohol use is one beer on Friday and occasionally Saturday.

**Objective:** BP 138/84 mmHg. Well appearing, afebrile. Musculoskeletal examination demonstrates synovitis of six MCP joints and both wrists, with additional MCP/PIP tenderness and tenderness of left second and third MTP joints. Right elbow and left ankle are tender without large effusion. Knees are cool without swelling. No rash or oral ulceration. Laboratory studies from 04/11/2026: hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, WBC 6.1 x10^3/uL, platelets 248 x10^3/uL, AST 26 U/L, ALT 31 U/L, creatinine 0.94 mg/dL, all within DMARD monitoring parameters; CRP elevated at 14.8 mg/L.

**Assessment:**
1. Seropositive rheumatoid arthritis with moderate inflammatory flare after interruption of methotrexate, supported by synovitis and elevated CRP.
2. Long-term methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine therapy requiring hematologic, hepatic, renal, and retinal monitoring; no current laboratory toxicity.
3. Essential hypertension, mildly above usual control, with possible transient worsening during glucocorticoid treatment.
4. GERD and prior NSAID intolerance.

**Plan:** Continue methotrexate 20 mg orally once weekly on Sunday; explicitly reviewed that methotrexate must never be taken daily. Renew a 90-day supply and coordinate pharmacy reminders/refill synchronization. Continue folic acid 1 mg daily except methotrexate day and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily. code.text: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast

DiagnosticReport.conclusion: Three-millimeter distal right ureteral calculus with mild hydroureteronephrosis. No additional acute abnormality.

dosageInstruction.text: Take one tablet by mouth twice daily with food as needed for pain for up to five days.
Take one capsule by mouth each evening for seven days; rise slowly because dizziness can occur.

ImagingStudy.description: Synthetic noncontrast CT abdomen and pelvis

transcript:
DR: Elena, I’m Dr. Shah. I know you have been waiting while we got your pain under control. Before we discuss the scan, tell me what happened tonight in your own words.
PT: I woke up around one with this sharp pain in my right back. It wrapped toward my lower belly and groin. I could not find any position that helped. I threw up twice, and my husband drove me here. It felt like the kidney stone I had six years ago, only faster and worse.
DR: At its worst, what number was the pain from zero to ten?
PT: A nine, maybe ten. After the IV medicine it is a three. I am finally able to sit still.
DR: Any burning when you urinate, needing to go more often, visible blood, fever, shaking chills, or trouble passing urine?
PT: No fever or chills. I did notice the urine looked pink in the cup here. Before that I had no burning, and I have been able to urinate.
DR: Any vaginal bleeding, unusual discharge, or chance of pregnancy?
PT: No. My last period started two weeks ago, and the pregnancy test here was negative.
DR: Good. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, diarrhea, or pain mainly on the right lower front of your abdomen?
PT: No. It starts in the back and comes in waves. My stomach is just sore from vomiting.
DR: You told the nurse you had one stone before. Did you pass it on your own? Was it analyzed?
PT: I passed it after three days. They gave me a strainer, but I never caught it. I did not need surgery and never saw a urologist.
DR: Do you have one kidney, kidney disease, gout, bowel disease, or prior abdominal surgery?
PT: No kidney disease. I still have both kidneys. No gout or bowel problems. I had my appendix out when I was a teenager.
DR: What medicines do you take, and do you have medication allergies?
PT: Sumatriptan only when a migraine starts and cetirizine during allergy season. No medication allergies. I took two ibuprofen tablets before coming, but I vomited soon afterward.
DR: Thank you. Your temperature is normal at 36.8 Celsius. Your first blood pressure was 148 over 86, likely elevated by pain. Your kidney function is normal; creatinine is 0.9. The urine has blood, which is common with a stone, but only two white cells, no nitrites, and no pattern suggesting infection. Your white blood cell count is not concerning.
PT: So it is definitely another stone?
DR: The noncontrast CT shows a three-millimeter stone in the lower right ureter, close to the bladder. It is causing mild backup of urine, called hydroureteronephrosis. A stone this size has a high likelihood of passing without a procedure. There is no other acute finding. Because you have no fever, your urine does not look infected, your kidney function is normal, and your pain and nausea improved, outpatient treatment is appropriate.
PT: Mild backup sounds scary. Could it damage my kidney?
DR: Temporary mild backup from a small stone usually resolves when it passes. The dangerous combination is obstruction plus infection, or obstruction with worsening kidney function, uncontrolled symptoms, or inability to urinate. You do not have those findings now. That is why the return precautions matter.
PT: What am I taking at home?
DR: Naproxen 500 milligrams twice daily with food as needed for pain, for no more than five days. Do not combine it with ibuprofen, Advil, Motrin, or other anti-inflammatory medicines. Stop it and seek advice if you develop black stools, vomiting blood, or severe stomach pain. You may use acetaminophen according to the package directions if needed, provided you do not have liver disease and are not taking another product containing acetaminophen.
PT: Okay. And the other prescription?
DR: Tamsulosin 0.4 milligrams each evening for seven days may relax the ureter and help passage. It can make you lightheaded, especially when standing. Take the first dose when you can be at home, rise slowly, and do not drive if you feel dizzy. We discussed that using it for stone passage is a short trial.
PT: Should I force a lot of water?
DR: Drink regularly so your urine stays pale, but do not force gallons quickly; that can worsen colicky pain. Small, steady amounts are fine. Use the strainer we are giving you whenever you urinate. If you catch the stone, let it dry in the container and bring it to follow-up for analysis.
PT: How will I know it passed?
DR: Often the waves of flank pain stop, and some people notice brief bladder pressure before seeing the stone. Symptoms stopping does not always prove passage. Call your primary care clinic tomorrow and arrange follow-up within one week. They can review symptoms and decide whether you need urology or repeat imaging. If you have not seen the stone and still have pain after a week, call promptly.
PT: I work at a bakery and have to stand. Can I go in tomorrow?
DR: I would rest tomorrow, especially because tamsulosin can cause dizziness and the pain could recur. Return to activity when pain is controlled, you are keeping fluids down, and you are not dizzy. Avoid driving while using any medicine that impairs you; the medicines prescribed today are not opioids, but symptoms themselves can still distract you.
PT: When do I come back here instead of waiting for the clinic?
DR: Return immediately for a temperature of 100.4 Fahrenheit or higher, shaking chills, worsening or unrelenting pain despite medicine, repeated vomiting or inability to keep fluids down, fainting, new weakness, inability to urinate, or feeling much sicker. Also return if you develop hives, swelling, or trouble breathing after a medication. Those could signal an infected obstruction or another emergency.
PT: My husband is in the waiting room. Is it okay for him to drive me?
DR: Yes, that is ideal. Before discharge we will make sure you can drink, walk safely, and urinate. The nurse will review the written instructions, prescriptions, and strainer.
PT: I can drink now. The nausea is almost gone. I am nervous the pain will hit nine again.
DR: It can come in waves while the stone moves. Take naproxen with food at the first return of pain if it is due and use a heating pad on low if that helps. If the pain remains severe after the medicine or feels different from tonight, come back. Do not assume every abdominal pain is the stone.
PT: Was there anything on the scan about my appendix area or ovaries?
DR: No acute abdominal or pelvic abnormality was reported beyond the right ureteral stone and mild backup. CT without contrast is designed primarily to find stones; if you develop new pelvic symptoms, bleeding, or focal front-right abdominal pain, you should be reevaluated.
PT: All right. I will call primary care, strain the urine, and come back for fever, vomiting, trouble urinating, or pain I cannot manage.
DR: Exactly. Your repeat vital signs and examination are reassuring, and you have a safe ride. This is a fully synthetic training encounter, not a real patient record, but the discharge plan is written as it would be for this scenario. Any last questions?
PT: No. Thank you for explaining the backup part without making it sound like nothing.
DR: You’re welcome. The nurse will bring the prescriptions and strainer, and we will discharge you once the oral-fluid check is complete.
note:
**Subjective:** Elena Navarro is a 37-year-old synthetic patient presenting to the emergency department with abrupt, severe right flank pain beginning at approximately 0100. Pain was colicky, radiated toward the right lower abdomen and groin, and reached 9–10/10. Associated symptoms included two episodes of nonbloody emesis and pink urine collected in the ED. She denied fever, rigors, dysuria, urinary frequency, inability to void, vaginal bleeding or discharge, chest pain, dyspnea, or diarrhea. Current pain is 3/10 after IV analgesia and hydration, with nausea nearly resolved. She reports one spontaneously passed stone six years ago without analysis or urologic procedure. No known chronic kidney disease, solitary kidney, gout, inflammatory bowel disease, or relevant surgery other than remote appendectomy. Home medications are intermittent sumatriptan and seasonal cetirizine. No known medication allergies. Pregnancy testing was negative.

**Objective:** Initial temperature 36.8 C and blood pressure 148/86 mmHg; repeat clinical assessment after analgesia was reassuring. Patient is alert, nontoxic, and now resting comfortably. Abdomen is soft without peritoneal findings; mild right costovertebral-angle tenderness is present. She tolerates oral fluid, ambulates steadily, and can void. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood and two WBC/HPF without nitrites or a pyuric pattern. Noncontrast CT abdomen/pelvis demonstrates a 3 mm distal right ureteral calculus with mild hydroureteronephrosis and no additional acute abnormality.

**Assessment:**
1. Acute right renal colic due to a 3 mm distal right ureteral stone with mild hydroureteronephrosis. Symptoms have improved with ED treatment. Small distal stone is likely to pass spontaneously.
2. Hematuria secondary to ureteral calculus. No current evidence of urinary infection, sepsis, acute kidney injury, anuria, or another indication for emergent decompression.

**Plan:** Discharge home with spouse after successful oral-fluid and ambulation checks. Start naproxen 500 mg by mouth twice daily with food as needed for pain for up to five days; avoid ibuprofen and all other NSAIDs while taking naproxen. May use acetaminophen per labeled dosing if needed and if no contraindication or duplicate acetaminophen product. Start tamsulosin 0.4 mg by mouth each evening for seven days as a short medical-expulsive-therapy trial; counsel regarding orthostatic dizziness, slow position changes, and avoiding driving if symptomatic. Encourage steady oral hydration without forced excessive intake. Provide urine strainer and specimen container; bring any recovered stone to follow-up for analysis. Call primary care tomorrow and arrange review within one week; consider urology referral or repeat imaging if symptoms persist, the stone is not observed to pass, or the clinical course changes. Return immediately for temperature at or above 100.4 F, shaking chills, escalating or uncontrolled pain, repeated vomiting or inability to retain fluids, fainting, inability to urinate, new weakness, medication reaction, or feeling significantly worse. Patient accurately teach-backed the medication limits, follow-up, and emergency precautions. This document describes a fully synthetic encounter and has not been clinically reviewed.
after_visit_summary:
Visit summary

What we found
• A 3 mm stone in the lower right ureter is causing renal colic and mild temporary urine backup.
• Kidney function is normal, and the urine does not currently suggest infection.

Medicines
• Naproxen 500 mg: take one tablet twice daily with food as needed for pain for up to 5 days. Do not take ibuprofen, Advil, Motrin, or another NSAID with it.
• Tamsulosin 0.4 mg: take one capsule each evening for 7 days. Rise slowly and do not drive if dizzy.

At home
• Drink steady amounts of fluid; do not force excessive water quickly.
• Strain every urine. Save any stone in the provided container and bring it to follow-up.
• Call primary care tomorrow for an appointment within 1 week.

Get emergency help now for
• Fever of 100.4 F or higher, shaking chills, worsening or uncontrolled pain, repeated vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, fainting, inability to urinate, new weakness, or an allergic reaction.

This is a fully synthetic, not clinically reviewed training summary.
