reasonCode.text: Expanding red tender area on left lower leg after scratching eczema

code.text: Nonpurulent cellulitis of left lower leg
Atopic dermatitis with excoriated ankle plaque

Observation.valueString: 8 x 11 cm warm erythematous tender patch above medial left ankle, no fluctuance, drainage, crepitus, bullae, or lymphangitic streaking; distal neurovascular status intact.

code.text: Skin cleansing, emollient dressing, and cellulitis border marking

dosageInstruction.text: Take one capsule by mouth four times daily for five days; complete the full course.
After redness is clearly improving, apply a thin layer twice daily to intact itchy eczema skin around, but not on, open or infected skin for up to seven days.

transcript:
PA: Hi, I’m Jordan, one of the physician assistants. I see you are here for redness on the left leg. What did you first notice?
PT: Two nights ago the skin above my left ankle started itching where my eczema flares. I scratched it in my sleep. Yesterday it was a small red patch, maybe the size of my palm. Today it is wider, warm, and sore when my jeans rub it.
PA: Has the redness spread over hours, or has it stayed about the same today?
PT: It looked bigger this afternoon than when I woke up. I drew a pen mark myself, but the line was uneven. It has not raced up the leg.
PA: Any fever, chills, sweats, nausea, unusual fatigue, or feeling generally ill?
PT: No. I feel normal except for the leg. My temperature at home was 98.4.
PA: Any pus, blister, boil, bite, cut, puncture, or drainage? Did you shave there recently or soak in a hot tub?
PT: No boil or pus. There are scratch marks and one tiny spot that bled. I did not see a bite. I shaved about a week ago, and no hot tub.
PA: How painful is it from zero to ten? Can you walk and move the ankle normally?
PT: About a four when I touch it, two otherwise. I walked here and can move the ankle. The calf itself does not hurt.
PA: Any swelling of the whole leg, calf tightness, recent long travel, surgery, immobilization, prior blood clot, chest pain, or shortness of breath?
PT: No. I flew to Denver last month, but nothing recent. No clot history, chest pain, or breathing issue. The swelling is just a little around the red skin.
PA: Have you had cellulitis or an abscess before? Any MRSA history?
PT: I had an infected hangnail years ago, never MRSA. Nothing like this on my leg.
PA: I want to verify allergies. Your chart says a sulfa antibiotic caused hives when you were a teenager. Any swelling, breathing trouble, or hospitalization? And have you taken penicillin or cephalexin?
PT: It was hives from trimethoprim-sulfa, no breathing trouble. I have taken amoxicillin for a tooth and did fine. I think I had cephalexin after the hangnail without a problem.
PA: Do you have diabetes, circulation problems, immune suppression, kidney disease, or pregnancy possibility?
PT: No diabetes or kidney disease. I am not on immune medicines. Pregnancy is not possible. I have asthma and eczema.
PA: What do you use for the eczema?
PT: Triamcinolone ointment when it gets bad and unscented lotion when I remember. I ran out of the ointment last month. I use albuterol maybe once every couple of months.
PA: Let me examine the leg. I am going to compare both sides and check the pulses. The red area is about eight by eleven centimeters above the inside of the left ankle. It is warm and mildly tender. I see superficial scratch marks and an eczema plaque, but no pocket that feels fluctuant, no pus, blistering, crackling under the skin, black color, or red streak tracking upward. Your ankle moves fully. Calf is soft and not tender. Foot is warm, pulse is strong, and sensation is normal.
PT: Does that mean it is cellulitis?
PA: Yes, this looks like uncomplicated nonpurulent cellulitis, probably bacteria entering through skin broken by scratching. Your temperature is 37.1 Celsius, heart rate 84, and you look well. I do not see an abscess to drain, signs of deep tissue infection, or findings that strongly suggest a blood clot. That makes oral antibiotics and close observation reasonable.
PT: Which antibiotic? I want to avoid the one that caused hives.
PA: Cephalexin 500 milligrams by mouth four times a day for five days. It is not a sulfonamide. Your prior tolerance is reassuring. Take the first dose today and finish all twenty capsules unless a clinician tells you to stop. You can take it with food if it upsets your stomach.
PT: Four times a day is hard. Does it have to be every six hours overnight?
PA: Space four doses across your waking day as evenly as practical—breakfast, lunch, dinner, and bedtime is a workable schedule. Do not take two doses at once. If you miss one and it is close to the next, skip the missed dose and return to the schedule.
PT: What reactions should I watch for?
PA: Mild nausea or loose stool can occur. Stop and seek emergency help for trouble breathing, facial or tongue swelling, widespread hives, faintness, or a severe rapidly developing reaction. Call promptly for severe or persistent watery diarrhea, blood in stool, or significant abdominal pain.
PT: Will it look better tomorrow?
PA: It may not. Cellulitis can look unchanged or slightly larger during the first 24 hours even after treatment starts. I am marking a clean border and writing the time. Elevate the leg above heart level when resting. A cool damp cloth may help comfort. Do not massage it, puncture it, or soak it in a bath, pool, or hot tub. Keep the scratched spot clean with gentle soap and water, pat dry, and cover loosely only if clothing rubs.
PT: Can I go to my restaurant shift tomorrow? I am on my feet for eight hours.
PA: If possible, take tomorrow off so you can elevate the leg and monitor the border. If you must work, avoid prolonged standing, take elevation breaks, and stop if pain or swelling worsens. Do not share towels. This is not generally contagious through casual contact, but open drainage should be covered.
PT: What about the eczema ointment?
PA: Do not apply steroid directly over the actively infected red area or the open scratch today. Use plain fragrance-free moisturizer on dry intact skin. Once the redness is clearly improving, you may apply a thin layer of triamcinolone 0.1 percent twice daily to intact itchy eczema skin around the area, not to open or infected skin, for up to seven days. Then stop and continue moisturizer.
PT: Should I take pain medicine?
PA: Acetaminophen according to the package directions is reasonable if you have no liver disease and are not taking another medicine containing it. Avoid using leftover antibiotics or topical antibiotic mixtures.
PT: When should somebody look at it again?
PA: We want a recheck in 48 hours, sooner if it worsens. You can return here or see primary care. Bring the written instructions and keep the border visible. At the recheck, we expect no further spread, less warmth or pain, and no new systemic symptoms.
PT: What sends me to the emergency room tonight?
PA: Go now for rapid spread well beyond the border, severe or pain out of proportion to the skin appearance, fever of 100.4 Fahrenheit or higher, shaking chills, confusion, fainting, repeated vomiting, red streaks moving toward the groin, new blisters, dusky or black skin, numbness, inability to move the ankle, or swelling of the entire leg. Also seek emergency help for chest pain or shortness of breath, or a serious allergic reaction.
PT: And if it just creeps a little past the line tomorrow?
PA: A small early change can happen, but call us the same day for any spread after you have started treatment, especially if pain or warmth increases. Rapid spread or systemic symptoms means the emergency department. If it is not clearly improving after 48 hours, it needs reassessment even if you otherwise feel well.
PT: Do I need a culture or blood test?
PA: There is no drainage to culture, and routine blood testing is unlikely to change treatment in a well-appearing person with a localized infection. If you develop fever, fail oral treatment, or form an abscess, evaluation changes and tests may be appropriate.
PT: Let me repeat it. Cephalexin four times daily for five days, starting today. Elevate, keep it clean and dry, no soaking, and recheck in two days. Emergency room for fast spreading, fever, severe pain, streaks, blisters, dark skin, or feeling sick.
PA: Exactly. Also remember the sulfa allergy remains documented, and cephalexin is a different antibiotic. We have reviewed the rare severe allergy signs. This is a fully synthetic training encounter rather than a real patient record. Within the scenario, you are stable for outpatient care.
PT: That makes sense. I will pick up the prescription now and ask my manager to cover tomorrow.
PA: Good. I have outlined the redness, placed a simple emollient dressing over the scratch, and printed the 48-hour recheck instructions. Please return sooner if anything concerns you.
note:
**Subjective:** Chinwe Okafor is a 29-year-old synthetic patient presenting to urgent care for two days of progressive erythema, warmth, and tenderness above the medial left ankle. Symptoms began after nocturnal scratching of an atopic dermatitis flare; one superficial excoriation briefly bled. The erythematous area expanded from approximately palm-sized yesterday to its current size today. Pain is 2/10 at rest and 4/10 with contact. Patient denies fever, chills, malaise, nausea, vomiting, purulent drainage, boil, known bite, lymphangitic streaking, whole-leg edema, calf pain, chest pain, or dyspnea. They can bear weight and move the ankle fully. No diabetes, CKD, immune suppression, recent surgery or immobilization, or prior MRSA. Sulfonamide allergy caused hives without anaphylaxis; patient previously tolerated amoxicillin and recalls tolerating cephalexin. Home treatment includes moisturizer; triamcinolone supply is exhausted.

**Objective:** Temperature 37.1 C, heart rate 84/min; patient is well appearing and ambulatory. An 8 x 11 cm warm, erythematous, mildly tender patch overlies the medial distal left lower leg with an excoriated eczema plaque. No fluctuance, purulence, bullae, crepitus, necrosis, lymphangitic streaking, or pain out of proportion. Calf is soft and nontender. Ankle has full range of motion without joint-centered pain. Foot is warm with strong distal pulse, normal sensation, and no diffuse unilateral edema. Border was marked and timed.

**Assessment:**
1. Uncomplicated nonpurulent cellulitis of the left lower leg, likely entering through excoriated eczematous skin. Patient has no systemic toxicity, drainable abscess, neurovascular compromise, deep-tissue warning sign, or clinical pattern suggesting DVT.
2. Atopic dermatitis with excoriation, contributing to impaired skin barrier.
3. Documented sulfonamide allergy; prescribed cephalexin is not a sulfonamide, and prior beta-lactam tolerance was confirmed.

**Plan:** Begin cephalexin 500 mg orally four times daily for five days, starting today, and complete all 20 capsules unless directed otherwise. Space doses across waking hours; do not double a missed dose. Take with food if needed for stomach upset. Seek emergency help for breathing difficulty, facial or tongue swelling, generalized hives, faintness, or another severe reaction; call promptly for severe or persistent watery diarrhea, bloody stool, or significant abdominal pain. Elevate the leg above heart level when resting. Keep excoriation clean with gentle soap and water, pat dry, and loosely cover if clothing rubs. Do not massage, puncture, or soak the area. A cool damp compress and labeled acetaminophen dosing may be used if otherwise safe.

Avoid topical steroid on active cellulitis or open skin. After infection is clearly improving, apply a thin layer of triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily only to intact itchy eczema skin around the area for up to seven days; continue fragrance-free emollient. Recheck in 48 hours here or with primary care, sooner for worsening. Go to the ED for rapid spread beyond the marked border, fever at or above 100.4 F, rigors, confusion, syncope, vomiting, severe or disproportionate pain, ascending red streaks, bullae, dusky or black skin, numbness, inability to move the ankle, whole-leg swelling, chest pain, or dyspnea. Any spread after antibiotics warrants same-day contact; lack of clear improvement by 48 hours requires reassessment. Patient completed accurate teach-back. This is a fully synthetic encounter and has not been clinically reviewed.
after_visit_summary:
Visit summary

What we found
• Cellulitis, a bacterial skin infection, on the left lower leg. There is no abscess to drain and no current sign of severe infection.
• Scratched eczema likely allowed bacteria through the skin.

Medicines
• Cephalexin 500 mg: take one capsule four times daily for 5 days, starting today. Finish all 20 capsules and do not double missed doses.
• Once redness is clearly improving, triamcinolone 0.1% may be used twice daily for up to 7 days on intact itchy eczema skin around the area—not on open or infected skin.

At home
• Elevate the leg, gently clean and dry the scratch, and avoid massage, puncture, or soaking.
• Keep the marked border visible. Recheck here or with primary care in 48 hours.

Get emergency help now for
• Rapid spread, fever of 100.4 F or higher, chills, confusion, fainting, vomiting, severe pain, red streaks, blisters, dark skin, numbness, inability to move the ankle, whole-leg swelling, chest pain, shortness of breath, or a severe allergic reaction.
